SportsTab.title: BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026: Cast your vote now
SportsTab.text:
Voting is now open for the BBC World Service Women's Footballer of the Year 2026.

Fans worldwide can vote from the five-player shortlist of Temwa Chawinga, Ewa Pajor, Alexia Putellas, Alessia Russo and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw.

The vote closes on Wednesday, 18 November at 09:00 GMT.

For the first time in the award's history, the winner will be announced as part of the BBC's Sports Personality of the Year on Sunday, 13 December as well as on the BBC World Service and the BBC Sport website and app.

Contenders for the award - now in its 12th year - are nominated by coaches, journalists and former professionals. It covers the period September 2025-August 2026.

Cast your vote, and read more on the five contenders.

Age: 28 Country: Malawi

Club: Kansas City Position: Forward

Chawinga has established herself as one of the world's most prolific forwards.

Her impact on the National Women's Soccer League is clear. Her extraordinary form helped Kansas City Current clinch the NWSL Shield as the league's top team in the regular season.

Chawinga scored 15 goals in the 2025 season as she became the first player to be named NWSL MVP in back-to-back campaigns. She also won the Golden Boot for the second year in a row.

Those performances earned her a contract extension through until 2029.

Chawinga returned to international football with Malawi for the 2026 Women's Africa Cup of Nations.

Alongside her sister Tabitha, she helped Malawi reach the country's first Wafcon final and - in doing so - qualify for the Women's World Cup for the first time.

Chawinga scored against Nigeria, Egypt, Ghana and Algeria at Wafcon, winning the tournament's Golden Boot with five goals.

Age: 29 Country: Poland

Club: Barcelona Position: Forward

Pajor is widely regarded as a world-class number nine - and it's clear why.

Instrumental as Barcelona won four trophies last season, Pajor scored their first two goals in a 4-0 Champions League final victory over Lyon.

The goals meant she finished as the competition's top scorer, while the result meant she won the Champions League for the first time after losing in five finals - four with Wolfsburg and one with Barcelona.

Pajor also enjoyed an outstanding second season with Barcelona in Liga F, scoring 16 league goals in her 23 appearances and providing five assists. She was a key player as Barca won the domestic treble.

On the international stage, Pajor captains Poland as is the team's leading goalscorer.

Age: 32 Country: Spain

Club: London City Lionesses Position: Midfielder

Putellas showed again this year why she is one of the most influential footballers in the world.

After 14 years with Barcelona, she delivered a spectacular final season with the club - helping them win four major trophies.

Her 14 goal contributions in 11 Champions League appearances helped her childhood club win the competition for the fourth time, and she remained a decisive figure bringing experience and leadership when it mattered most.

Putellas delayed announcing her move to London City Lionesses to avoid creating a distraction, but in July 2026 she completed that transfer, saying the club's "women-only identity and ambition" were important factors.

Internationally, Putellas was instrumental in Spain retaining the Women's Nations League in late 2025, scoring three goals against Sweden in the semi-finals before being named player of the finals as Spain defeated Germany 3–0.

Last month she was awarded a record-equalling third Ballon d'Or.

Age: 29 Country: Jamaica

Club: Manchester City Position: Forward

After a fine year, Shaw has positioned herself as one of the world's elite forwards.

The defining striker in Manchester City's Women Super League title-winning campaign, she scored 21 goals in 22 league appearances, won a record third consecutive WSL Golden Boot and was named WSL Player of the Season.

Her goals were central to City ending a 10-year wait for the league title.

They went on to complete the Double, with Shaw scoring the opening goal in their FA Cup final victory over Brighton at Wembley to finish the season with 26 goals in all competitions.

She also reached a major personal milestone in December 2025 when she became the first player in the history of City's professional women's team to score 100 goals.

Amid uncertainty over her future, Shaw announced at City's end-of-season celebrations that she had signed a new four-year contract through to 2030.

SportsTab.title: England: James Hill called up as cover for Ezri Konsa for Croatia Nations League game
SportsTab.text:
Bournemouth defender James Hill has been called up to the England squad for the first time.

The 24-year-old centre-back has been added to Thomas Tuchel's squad after Arsenal's Ezri Konsa was ruled out of Thursday's Nations League match against Croatia at Wembley.

Konsa was substituted after sustaining a knee injury in the Champions League win at Slavia Prague on Wednesday, but played all 90 minutes of the win over Hull on Saturday.

He will return to full training this week, before England's game against Spain in Madrid on Sunday.

On Sunday Dan Burn replaced centre-back Marc Guehi, who withdrew with a hip injury.

Hill has played every minute of Bournemouth's Premier League season and has featured in every game of their inaugural Europa League campaign.

He joined Bournemouth from Fleetwood for an undisclosed fee in January 2022.

Having made only 24 appearances in his first three and a half years with the club, Hill became a regular last season as Bournemouth achieved their highest top-flight finish of sixth.

Bournemouth, who are on an eight-match winning run in all competitions, are seventh in the Premier League.

SportsTab.title: Felix Nmecha celebration: Borussia Dortmund fans' group criticises midfielder
SportsTab.text:
A Christian group for footballers says it wants to "demonstrate love and respect towards everyone" following criticism from Borussia Dortmund fans of midfielder Felix Nmecha's goal celebration.

A supporters' group said it objected to Nmecha's goal celebration because it referenced a campaign by Ballers in God called 'The King's Return'.

The supporters' group said, external the campaign discriminates against homosexuality and transgender people, paints abortion as "Satan's plan" and is at odds with Dortmund's values of tolerance and respecting diversity.

To celebrate his two goals in the 2-1 win over Elversberg on Saturday, Nmecha pointed to the sky and mimed taking a crown off his head and placing it on the ground.

He said there were "misunderstandings" over his celebration and that it was "not intended to promote myself or any organisation".

Citing a recent investigation by German broadcaster ARD, the fans' group said "extremely conservative positions against homosexuality and transgender identity are advocated" by the campaign.

Ballers in God, external was created by former Crystal Palace and Tottenham midfielder John Bostock.

The organisation promotes Christian beliefs and has high-profile followers such as England's Marc Guehi and Bukayo Saka and former Brazil forward Kaka.

In response to the supporters' group's claims, Ballers in God said: "We are encouraged by player-led movements such as The King's Return, where footballers themselves take the initiative to express their faith in Jesus.

"Our desire is not only to share our hope, but to demonstrate love and respect towards everyone, including those who do not share our beliefs.

"Our focus has always been, and will always be, to point people to Jesus with grace and love."

Nmecha said: "My message has never been about promoting intolerance, discrimination, or hate in any form."

Last year the Premier League withdrew from the Rainbow Laces campaign and ended its partnership with LGBTQ+ charity Stonewall.

In 2024 then Ipswich captain Sam Morsy, a Muslim, said he did not wear a rainbow armband because of his "religious beliefs".

Guehi wrote "I [heart] Jesus" on his rainbow armband when he captained Palace.

Manchester United abandoned plans to wear a jacket supporting the LGBTQ+ community because a player refused.

SportsTab.title: Bryson DeChambeau: American running out of options after LIV Golf collapse, says Rory McIlroy
SportsTab.text:
Rory McIlroy says the addition of Bryson DeChambeau to the DP World Tour next season would bring more "eyeballs" to the tour but feels the American is running out of options.

DeChambeau's competitive future is uncertain following the collapse of LIV Golf, with the two-time US Open champion last week saying he will approach his next move with "humility and respect".

The 33-year-old American can apply for DP World Tour membership based on his status as a recent major champion, which would offer him the chance to earn back his PGA Tour card for 2028.

"I think a name like Bryson DeChambeau and everything he brings with him, good and bad, he brings eyeballs, which is a good thing for tournaments," said McIlroy, who was pipped to the 2024 US Open in dramatic fashion by DeChambeau.

"Honestly, I'm certainly not in his shoes, and nor would I ever want to be but it doesn't seem like he's got many options.

"You know, if he wants to play competitive golf, it doesn't seem like he's got many options."

Northern Ireland's McIlroy was speaking to reporters in Dubai before the DP World Tour Championship as he chases a record-equalling eighth season-long title.

The six-time major winner trails Spain's Eugenio Chacarra by 533 points in the Race to Dubai standings going into the final event in Dubai, which offers 2,000 points to the winner.

Nine players - Chacarra, McIlroy, Patrick Reed, Casey Jarvis, Aaron Rai, Jon Rahm, Ryan Fox, Jayden Schaper and Daniel Hillier - can still clinch the Race to Dubai title, but McIlroy would guarantee his fifth straight crown with victory at Jumeirah Golf Estates this week.

McIlroy's excellent record at the Dubai tournament includes three wins and a play-off defeat by England's Matt Fitzpatrick last year.

"I'm very excited to be back here, very excited to be in contention for the eighth," said the 37-year-old.

"I made some ground up last week, maybe not as much as I wanted, but I felt like it was a step in the right direction.

"Getting back to a place where I played, I played well and I had a lot of success, even last year in the play-off with Matt, it's been a course that's been very good to me over the years, and I have a lot of experience on it and a lot of experience up at the top end of the leaderboard."

SportsTab.title: F1 Q&A: How good is Hamilton and how long can he stay in F1?
SportsTab.text:
McLaren's Lando Norris converted pole position into a race win at a wet-dry-wet Sao Paulo Grand Prix on Sunday.

Max Verstappen came through the field to take second after starting at the back of the grid because of an engine penalty, while his Red Bull team-mate Isack Hadjar was on the podium in third.

Mercedes sealed the constructors' championship for the first time since 2021 at Interlagos following a fourth-place finish for George Russell and fifth for new world champion Kimi Antonelli.

Here BBC F1 correspondent Andrew Benson answers your latest questions.

Lewis Hamilton has just completed his 400th F1 grand prix, with more than 100 of these races having him on pole position. There are drivers with a better pole percentage than this, so just how good is he and for how much longer can he stay at the top? - Clive

Lewis Hamilton is unquestionably one of the greatest Formula 1 drivers in history.

He's statistically the most successful - with the most race wins and pole positions.

He's tied with Michael Schumacher for the most championships with seven, and many would - and do - argue he should have eight, given the controversy of the mishandled final race of the 2021 season.

Greatness as an F1 driver is about more than raw statistics, but even so Hamilton has consistently proved to be at the very highest level, with a series of outstanding drives in races that will go down in history as some of the greatest ever.

Examples of those would be the 2008 British Grand Prix and the 2021 Brazilian Grand Prix, along with many others.

All of this should go without saying.

He's also won races in nearly all his seasons - the only exceptions being 2022, 2023 and 2025.

There is no question that, within the context of his remarkable career, Hamilton struggled relatively in the era of 'ground-effect' cars from 2022-25.

He was beaten by Mercedes team-mate George Russell in two of their three seasons together, and looked a shadow of his usual self against Charles Leclerc in 2025.

Those performances led some to question why a driver formerly famed and lauded for his adaptability did not seem as able to adapt to the driving style required of those cars.

And that, in turn, led to questions as to whether the fact he apparently could not was related to his age - he is now 41.

But with this year's cars, Hamilton is back in much more familiar territory, is performing extremely well again and is neck-and-neck with Leclerc.

Those questions about the four years from 2022-25 will remain just that, but there is no doubt Hamilton is sensitive to them. He has referenced them a number of times this year, including last weekend in Brazil, when the topic of his 400th race came up.

"I never ever thought that I would be reaching numbers like that," he said. "It's crazy because I still feel young, and regardless of the things that people say, you saw my pole last week, I still have the pace, I still have the speed and I still have the dedication, which is most important and the focus. For me, that number is kind of irrelevant."

Longevity in sport depends on many factors, and each athlete is different.

On the face of it, however, there is no obvious reason why, on an age front, Hamilton cannot continue for a good few more years - Fernando Alonso is 45 and is still performing at an extremely high level, as he proved yet again in Brazil at the weekend.

Hamilton has said he wants to race at least until F1 returns to Africa, which will not be until 2030 at the earliest, when he, too, will be 45.

For that, he will need at least one new contract, as his current one with Ferrari is believed to end next year.

We heard, and saw, a lot of 'yo-yo racing' in the first half of the season. This seems to have reduced. What has changed? - Ali

'Yo-yo racing' was a term coined at the start of this year for a new character of on-track battle in which cars swapped positions multiple times over a series of laps.

This was caused by the new power-units introduced this year, which have a near 50-50 split between internal combustion and electrical power and are fundamentally energy starved.

The operations of these engines included 'overtake' and 'boost' modes.

'Boost' is a facility for a driver to demand extra electrical energy whenever he wants, as long as the battery has charge.

'Overtake' mode gives a driver following within one second of a car in front an extra 0.5MJ of energy recovery and deployment capability per lap.

At the start of the season, this - combined with the teams' and drivers' relative unfamiliarity with the new technology - led to a number of examples of yo-yo racing in the early grands prix.

This is where one driver has more electrical energy available, uses it to overtake, whereupon the driver behind now has more and overtakes back, and so on.

This has been less prevalent recently and there are two reasons for that.

Primarily, the tracks in recent weeks have been less 'energy-starved'. And the more energy-starved a car is at a track, the more likelihood there is for yo-yo racing.

The overtaking comes from the variation in energy levels, and being at tracks where drivers can't use all the energy they want all the time.

On top of that, drivers and teams have now been using the engines for a season and are much more on top of how to use them, and therefore how not to leave themselves vulnerable.

At the same time, rule changes have been introduced since the start of the season to reduce the impact of energy starvation, such as imposing energy limits on tracks where it is a major issue. This flattens out the peaks and troughs in energy availability.

And into next year and beyond further steps are being taken to make the engines more "normal" in operation - by changing the energy split to 60-40 in two steps by 2028.

This is almost certainly going to lead to the frequency of overtaking reducing, while the drivers become happier with how the cars feel to drive.

Whether the audience perceives that as better or worse racing remains to be seen.

What is the reason a driver like Esteban Ocon would want to stay in F1 as a reserve driver rather than commit to race elsewhere in a different series? All F1 drivers are very, very good, and presumably would be in demand, so why not compete elsewhere, win some races, be a hero? - Stephen

When it became clear that Ocon was not going to be retained by Haas next year, and that his options for a race seat seemed to have evaporated, the Frenchman was insistent that his F1 career was not over.

Staying involved in the sport as a reserve driver - if he can find a spot - is the best way to keep current in the sport.

It means a driver is available should either of the race drivers at whatever team he can land with be incapacitated.

It keeps him familiar with current F1 machinery through simulator sessions, and perhaps driving recent cars.

And it simply keeps his face around and in people's minds.

Go and race elsewhere, whether it's Indycar, Formula E or endurance racing, for example, and it's much easer to be forgotten, or for people to assume your time has come and gone.

Why hasn't Liam Lawson been confirmed for 2027 despite his brilliant driving this year? - Pete

The decision as to which two of the three drivers in contention to drive for Racing Bulls next year is in the hands of the Red Bull shareholders Chalerm Yoovidhya and Mark Mateschitz, and Red Bull's ultimate F1 boss Oliver Mintzlaff.

Lawson is in contention along with his current team-mate Arvid Lindblad and F2 front-runner Nikola Tsolov.

The old Red Bull way - under Helmut Marko and Christian Horner - would have been to jettison Lawson now on the basis he has had his chance in the lead team and is unlikely to be considered for another, and put in Tsolov as the next cab off the rank, so to speak.

The counter-argument is that leaves two unproven talents going against each other next year, which would leave Red Bull not knowing what they are looking at.

Better, this argument goes, to keep Lawson and Lindblad together next year for a fuller reading on Lindblad, with Lawson as a known-quantity benchmark, then drop whoever performs least well at the end of 2027 in favour of Tsolov.

In not so many words, Racing Bulls team boss Alan Permane made this second argument in Brazil at the weekend.

"Red Bull's had a very successful young driver programme," he said, "and I don't want to be critical of it, but I think if you guys are critical of it, maybe sometimes the drivers haven't been able to have enough time to settle, or maybe some snap decisions have been made.

"We're trying to apply a little bit of science, and that takes some time.

"So we are looking at everything and studying, analysing, and time is on our side. We're not in a rush to do anything, and I'm very confident the right decision will be made.

"I realise it's frustrating for our drivers. I realise it's frustrating for everyone else, but we want to get it right, and we will get it right."

Interlagos consistently produces thrilling races. Should F1 be doing more to preserve racing at 'classic' circuits? - Nathan

F1 faces a difficult balancing act with the calendar.

It wants a truly global world championship. It wants exciting racing that engages audiences. It wants a good mix of circuit types for variation and interest. And it wants to make money.

When it comes to 'classic' race tracks, that's not always an easy equation to solve.

The main reason is that the classic tracks are often in countries that are not able or willing to pay the big-money fees.

The same model and restrictions do not apply in autocracies that want to use races for national self-promotion, hence they can and do tend to pay bigger fees.

But F1 is well aware of the importance of classic circuits, and it wants to ensure it keeps the best of them.

As a consequence, F1 does make compromises that ensure the likes of Monaco, Silverstone, Spa and Suzuka stay on the calendar, even if not every year any more in the case of Spa.

At the same time, the sport makes a considerable effort to make new tracks as interesting as possible. Some are more successful than others, but that's always going to be the case.

Take Las Vegas, for example. It is far from the greatest track in terms of driving challenge, and was hardly likely to be given it is made up of streets in an American city, but it makes up for that with spectacle and kudos.

As for forthcoming permanent circuits, former F1 driver Alex Wurz - the designer of the new tracks in Qiddiyah, Saudi Arabia, and Rwanda, which are both due to come on to the calendar in the next few years - has done his level best to ensure they are fulfilling and challenging for drivers and promote good racing.

SportsTab.title: Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup: Spectacular England still short of best form
SportsTab.text:
Rob Hawkins laughed when asked by BBC Sport whether he had been practising his dives.

The question was prompted by some spectacular athleticism as he scored five tries to help England crush Australia 86-18 in Tuesday's Wheelchair Rugby League World Cup semi-final in Wollongong, Australia.

"It's just off-the-cuff stuff when needed," he said. "Some of the kicks were cautious!"

The man who had provided many of those kicks, Nathan Collins, was sitting beside him. He did not disagree.

"He makes my bad kicks look good!" Collins said. "It is great to have him there to sweep up. He's great to play with and against."

England have reason to be in good spirits as they prepare for a fifth successive World Cup final, the fourth in a row against great rivals France.

They are looking to defend the title they won on home ground four years ago, a narrow 28-24 victory in Manchester.

All of the three previous finals between the two teams have been tight: France won 42-40 in Gillingham in 2013, and 38-34 in Perpignan in 2017.

England seemed to set themselves up perfectly for Friday's final, scoring 15 tries against Australia. Hawkins' five scores, plus five conversions, took his personal points tally to 30 points.

His best try, and the standout from the whole game, was the third one - a long-range punt from England seemed to be a shot to nothing, but not where Hawkins was concerned.

He chased it down and, millimetres away from the dead-ball line, managed to grab the ball and get it down under huge pressure from Adam Tannock, who he had outpaced.

Yet Hawkins thought his and England's performances were far from perfect.

"Wouldn't say we are 10 out of 10 yet, there are still good a good few things to look at," he said. "Today was a six or seven. Hopefully the best is to come on Friday.

"Today was satisfying but not easy. We had the crowd to fight and a ruthless Australian team. But we are happy with the result."

England will now reset for their latest showdown with France, which will kick off at 08:45 GMT on Friday at WIN Entertainment Centre.

Collins said England will need to repeat their dominant performance against Australia, and more, to beat the only other nation ever to win the world title.

"We've got to do what we did today, stick to the process Tom [Coyd, the England coach] has put in front of us," he said. "It looks like a good game, but there is still plenty to do.

"We are used to big games, league titles and Challenge Cups. This is a step up from that, so we go again."

Like many of the squad, Collins has had to overcome huge off-field challenges to get in a position to face the major challenges on the pitch.

Born with dwarfism, he played running rugby league as a child before being told he was too small. So, Collins moved into the wheelchair sport and made his England debut aged 16.

Now 26, he is a veteran of the team preparing for his third World Cup final, having won one, lost one.

"It has given me a lease of life," Collins said of his life in rugby league. "I have met so many amazing people along the way.

"At 16 I was straight in at the deep end, I couldn't think about it, just had to do it. Not many people get those chances at 16. I have grown with the game, I feel like I have gone on the level up with it.

"I'm proud of what we have achieved, on and off the pitch. It would mean a lot to bring that trophy home again.

"Looking in the corner of the stadium and seeing the wall of white [shirted England fans], it was amazing, hopefully we will see that again on Friday."

England will hope it is only the French players they have to deal with in the final, after bizarre scenes involving an official in 2022.

French referee Laurent Abrial, who officiated the 2022 World Cup final, was suspended until January this year after he "brought the game into disrepute through unacceptable behaviour".

An International Rugby League misconduct committee found Abrial made "obscene gestures that could have incited the crowd".

Abrial was the defence referee during the final and in the closing stages protested by gesticulating wildly after having a decision overruled by attack referee Ollie Cruickshank.

"The referees will make a decision on the day, we are just there to play the game," said Hawkins. "Our win overshadowed the decisions made. The officiating at this World Cup has been superb."

SportsTab.title: Mauricio Pochettino interested in leaving USMNT job for Manchester United
SportsTab.text:
US men’s national team head coach Mauricio Pochettino is interested in a move to Manchester United, multiple sources told the Guardian, with those same sources characterizing the interest as mutual.

United are expected to sack their head coach, Michael Carrick, after a disastrous start to their season which leaves them at risk of relegation from the Premier League, their worst opening to a campaign in four decades.

Securing Pochettino’s services is far from simple or inexpensive. The Argentinian’s contract contains a release clause in the neighborhood of $10m (£7.5m), multiple sources familiar with the deal told the Guardian this week, a figure that grows should United choose to retain Pochettino’s staff, including his longtime assistant and confidant Jesús Pérez, who has worked with Pochettino for 16 years. The Athletic first reported the details of Pochettino’s buyout.

Pochettino was brought on by the US in 2024 and guided the USMNT to a last-16 finish at the 2026 World Cup, by most accounts a disappointment. US Soccer brought him back through 2030, with both sides expressing a mutual belief and commitment towards not only brightening the fortunes of the US men but also overhauling the federation’s approach towards youth development.

“Every time we sign a contract, it’s to go to the last day of the contract,” Pochettino told reporters after his contract renewal. “If we sign a four-year contract, we need to think to arrive there. And we signed the contract because we really believe that we are going to be four years there. Because if not, it’s bad. If we don’t believe in that process, if we don’t believe in that journey, why sign [for] four years? Only to be sure that we are going to receive a salary at the end of the month? That is not nice. It’s not the way that we think. We really signed that contract because we really believe that we can arrive to the end.”

Pochettino, who has been linked with a host of high-profile club openings since his arrival in the United States, tempered those remarks by adding another: “In life, nothing is sure. Less in football.”

The USMNT are days from a pair of Concacaf Nations League matches against Haiti in Cincinnati and Miami, their first competitive fixtures of the 2030 qualifying cycle. Pochettino is scheduled to address reporters on Friday afternoon.

Why would Pochettino be interested?

Pochettino has repeatedly expressed his interest in returning to the Premier League during his time with the US. As recently as September, he spoke to Sky Sports about the idea of winning the league and “building a project with the possibility of winning”. In late 2025 he said much the same, telling the BBC he believed the league was the best in the world and adding “of course I am missing it. I am so happy in America but am thinking but also thinking one day to come back.”

Beyond his stated interest, Pochettino is also widely known as a coach who enjoys the day-to-day responsibilities of coaching and he’s widely regarded as an excellent man-manager who thrives in the daily rhythm of life at a club. He maintains a home in London and speaks glowingly of the UK and the football culture that permeates it. In short, there are no shortage of reasons for him to leave the US.

What would US Soccer do if he leaves?

Most federations have contingency plans developed for the departure of a head coach and the US federation is no exception, especially given the repeated interest in Pochettino over the years. Prior to bringing the Argentine on board, US Soccer reached out to or spoke to several other high-profile candidates, most notably former Liverpool and current Germany boss Jürgen Klopp.

In the nearer term, several domestic candidates could fit the bill – current U-23 head coach Steve Cherundolo being one. Nashville SC head coach (and former US interim head coach) BJ Callaghan could be another candidate close to home, having guided the MLS club to a league-record points total this season.

In some respects, there is no better time for Pochettino to depart; doing so now would allow an incoming coach the majority of a four-year cycle to work with and the federation itself would earn millions just months after Pochettino could’ve departed for free.

Is Pochettino likely to leave without his coaching staff?

That feels highly unlikely. Pochettino enjoys an unusually close relationship with his assistants, in particular his second-in-command, Jesús Pérez. Pérez has served alongside Pochettino at every stop in his coaching career, from La Liga side Espanyol in 2010 to stops at Southampton, Tottenham Hotspur, PSG and Chelsea in the 15 years that followed. It’s rare to see Pochettino anywhere in a professional capacity without Pérez at his side.

Pochettino has similarly close bonds with his other assistants – Miki D’Agostino, goalkeeper coach Toni Jiménez and several others. They, too, have been with the Argentine since the start.

SportsTab.title: NFL trade deadline 2026: Vikings eye Kirk Cousins reunion, Bengals-Eagles deal collapses – live updates
SportsTab.text:
The 49ers are sending a sixth-round pick in the 2027 draft to Indianapolis in exchange for Allen, according to reports. With San Francisco getting healthier at wide receiver, the 34-year-old provides experienced depth at a relatively modest price.

Colts trade WR Keenan Allen to 49ers

The San Francisco 49ers have acquired six-time Pro Bowl wide receiver Keenan Allen from the Indianapolis Colts, according to multiple reports, giving Brock Purdy another experienced target for the stretch run.

Allen, who had been seeking a move to a contender, joins a San Francisco team with inside track on the No 1 seed looking to bolster their passing attack ahead of the playoff push. The 34-year-old veteran brings more than a decade of NFL experience and one of the league’s most reliable pairs of hands. Terms of the deal have yet to emerge.

Updated at 14.01 EST

ESPN’s Adam Schefter reports that the Vikings have their trade target, and it’s Kirk Cousins.

The NFL reinstated Brandon Aiyuk on Monday and gave the 49ers a two-week roster exemption ⁠to determine their next step with the disgruntled former All-Pro wide receiver.

Aiyuk had been on the reserve/left squad list since December 2025, when he stopped reporting to the Niners while rehabbing a knee injury.

It doesn’t sound like Aiyuk will be making any return to San Francisco – coach Kyle Shanahan said on Monday that the status change “means absolutely nothing to our team” – and they could attempt to trade him before today’s deadline. Will teams want to sign him given the fact that he hasn’t played a game since December 2024, and even during that season, he had just 374 receiving yards in seven games? The league also told Aiyuk and the players union last week that it believes he must repay the Niners $13m in already-paid bonuses for failing to participate in team activities.

His agent, Drew Rosenhaus, seems to believe a team will take the chance. On the Pat McAfee Show today, he said: “I think that in all likelihood Brandon will probably sign with a team that knows him, somebody that has somehow been affiliated with him either in college or the 49ers. That’s just my guess.”

The Falcons are signing kicker Jake Moody ⁠off the Ravens’ practice squad and releasing fellow Nick ⁠Folk, according to insider Jordan Schultz.

Moody had a 53-yard field goal and an extra point in his debut for the Ravens last Thursday. Folk, a 19-year veteran of the league, missed his fifth field-goal attempt of the season in Atlanta’s loss to the Bengals in Madrid on Sunday.

Updated at 13.11 EST

Who are the Vikings’ options on the quarterback market?

They have the best defense in the NFL and an excellent group of position players, headlined by wide receiver Justin Jefferson. A competent quarterback could be the difference between wasted windows and Super Bowl contention. Some of the names being thrown around:

Kirk Cousins (Raiders)

Daniel Jones (Colts)

Justin Herbert (Chargers)

Eagles-Bengals trade for DE Arnold Ebikeite falls through

With just under four hours until the deadline, we’ve gone from one trade on the day to minus-1. NFL insiders Ian Rapoport and Jordan Schultz report that the Bengals’ trade with the Eagles for Arnold Ebikeite has been called off.

Rapoport says it was scratched by the Bengals “with an eye toward keeping a future compensatory draft pick they would’ve lost with this deal” and that the agreement had not been finalized. That compensatory draft pick would have been the one the Bengals were to receive for former edge rusher Trey Hendrickson signing with Baltimore this year in free agency.

Updated at 12.59 EST

The Jaguars have reportedly received calls about wideout Brian Thomas Jr, but ESPN says they have told teams they aren’t interested and have no plans to trade him.

Thomas was the 23rd overall pick in the 2024 draft and had a breakout season as a rookie, with 87 catches for 1,282 yards and 10 touchdowns plus Pro Bowl honors. His production has dramatically dropped since: he has 10 catches for 117 yards and two touchdowns. He received zero targets from Jacksonville quarterback Trevor Lawrence in Thursday’s loss to the Ravens.

Updated at 12.22 EST

Not a trade, but an NFL development nonetheless: Dolphins defensive tackle Zach Sieler will undergo season-ending surgery on his ruptured biceps, per ESPN.

Sieler was hurt during Miami’s loss to the Lions. He had recorded 24 tackles and two sacks in eight games this season.

The Dolphins are 1-7 and stuck at the bottom of the AFC East standings. Sieler’s absence leaves a hole in their defensive line.

Updated at 11.58 EST

In NFL-adjacent news:

Jordon Hudson is suing two Airbnb hosts over a Ring doorbell camera video of a shirtless Bill Belichick. Hudson says that the 2023 clip invaded her privacy by prompting public disclosure of her relationship with the former Patriots coach.

The Lions strengthened their depleted secondary on Monday, trading for Jets safety Andre Cisco in exchange for a 2028 sixth-round pick. Cisco has played in nine games this season for New York but wasn’t a regular starter. Detroit are down two safeties in star Kerby Joseph, who is out with a knee injury, and Thomas Harper, who is on injured reserve.

The Bears made a trade with the Titans for defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons on 29 October. He’s hit the ground running in Chicago.

In his first two games, Simmons has two sacks, 10 tackles, three tackles for loss, two quarterback hits and two passes defended.

I’m sure you’ll hear more on this topic later today from the Guardian’s resident Philadelphian Bryan Armen Graham, but for now! After trading Arnold Ebiketie to the Bengals, the Eagles now up to 10 owned picks in the 2027 draft.

Philadelphia are in the middle of a seven-game losing streak, the franchise’s worst skid since 2012. General manager Howie Roseman is stocking up.

The Colts have had a busy few weeks. After a 2-4 start, they fired longtime GM Chris Ballard. They traded eight-time All-Pro guard Quenton Nelson and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner.

The big question is how much that fire sale continues today. There’s speculation Indianapolis could trade away star running back Jonathan Taylor or quarterback Daniel Jones – or even the both of them.

Several insiders around the NFL have said Taylor would command a high package – perhaps similar to what Christian McCaffrey went for when he was traded from the Panthers to the 49ers in 2022 for a second-, third- and fourth-round pick in the 2023 draft, plus a fifth-round pick in 2024. The Giants have been floated as a potential landing spot, but it’s unclear if they could give the Colts what they want.

Eagles trade DE Arnold Ebiketie to Bengals

The Eagles are still making moves, trading edge rusher Arnold Ebiketie to the Bengals for a 2027 sixth-round pick, per multiple reports.

A second-round pick by Atlanta in 2022, Ebiketie has 16.5 sacks in his career. He spent four seasons with the Falcons and then joined the Eagles this offseason on a one-year, $7.3m contract.

A team to watch today: the Minnesota Vikings. If you watched them on Monday night, you’ll know about their messy quarterback situation. Regular starter Kyler Murray is out with a hamstring injury; Carson Wentz, the 33-year-old veteran backup, was dreadful against the Bills, going 8-for-25 for 81 yards and three turnovers. His completion percentage was the worst by a quarterback with at least 10 attempts in a game this season.

Murray is considered week-to-week, but the offense has been mediocre even with him. Minnesota traded away JJ McCarthy, the player they had selected just two years ago with the No 10 overall pick, in September. The Vikings still have the NFL’s leading scoring defense, but their offense is an obvious weakness. After a 6-0 start, they have lost two straight.

Could a reunion with Kirk Cousins be in store? The 38-year-old is the starter for the Raiders, but they also have top draft pick Fernando Mendoza waiting in the wings. Do they try for Daniel Jones, who had a short stint as the Vikings’ third-stringer in 2024?

ESPN’s Adam Schefter and Ian Rapoport report that the Vikings have begun making calls around the league about trading for a quarterback.

Jaguars add DT Jordan Davis in trade with Eagles

AFC South leaders Jacksonville went all-in on Monday, adding defensive tackles Jordan Davis in a blockbuster trade with Philadelphia. The Eagles got a 2027 first-round draft pick and a 2029 second-round pick in return.

Davis has just 1.5 sacks with one interception in nine games this season, but he had career highs in 2025 with 4.5 sacks and 72 tackles. He was a first-round draft pick in 2022 and helped the Eagles beat the Chiefs in Super Bowl LIX, receiving a three-year, $78m contact on the heels of that win.

Monday’s trade capped a trio of defensive moves by the Jaguars, who have won five of their last six games. They also traded for Falcons safety Jessie Bates III and for Saints defensive tackle Davon Godchaux.

In total, the Jaguars gave up six future draft picks. If the season ended today, they would be the No 3 seed in the AFC. They clearly think they can go higher.

Hello and welcome to our live coverage of the 2026 NFL trade deadline. After weeks of splashy moves, swirling rumors and increasingly frantic speculation, we’re finally approaching the moment of truth. The clock is ticking and all 32 teams have until 4pm ET (9pm GMT) to get their affairs in order.

It’s already been an eventful trading season. The Chicago Bears made the biggest splash by acquiring All-Pro defensive tackle Jeffery Simmons from the Tennessee Titans for a package including two first-round draft picks. The Jacksonville Jaguars made a trio of moves to bolster their defense, headlined by a trade with Philadelphia to land defensive tackle Jordan Davis. The Indianapolis Colts have been busy dismantling their roster, shipping eight-time Pro Bowl guard Quenton Nelson to Seattle and defensive tackle DeForest Buckner to San Francisco. Meanwhile, Marvin Harrison Jr has landed in Houston, Joey Porter Jr has joined Dallas and the injury-ravaged Baltimore Ravens have brought in veteran quarterback Jacoby Brissett.

But plenty of questions remain unanswered. Will Indianapolis continue their fire sale by parting with star running back Jonathan Taylor? Which contenders will make one last push for reinforcements? And could another blockbuster deal emerge before the window slams shut?

We’ll be following every confirmed trade, credible rumor and last-minute development throughout the day, with instant analysis of what the moves mean for the playoff race and beyond.

Strap in. Deadline day has arrived and there’s plenty still to play out.

TechnologyTab.title: Trump says FBI investigating Nvidia boss's affair with alleged Chinese spy
TechnologyTab.text:
US President Donald Trump has said the FBI is investigating the affair between the chief executive of Nvidia and an alleged Chinese spy.

Trump said he spoke to Jensen Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.

"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Beijing has rejected claims that Huang was targeted, with its foreign ministry saying the allegations were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Speaking later at a White House press briefing, Trump told reporters, "I know the FBI is looking into" the affair but did not give further details on the investigation, or confirm when it was launched.

Trump added he thought that Huang was an "honourable guy and I feel very confident that he will be in good shape" after the investigations.

The FBI declined to comment when contacted by the BBC.

Nvidia, which has commissioned an independent investigation into the affair involving Alice Huang, alleged to be a Chinese spy, said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised.

Nvidia is the world's second most valuable company after Apple, and designs computer chips that have become central to AI technology.

The revelations knocked about $250bn (£190bn) off Nvidia's value on Monday as the company's share price fell by more than 4%.

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report. She is not related to Jensen Huang.

According to the newspaper, Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington in spring this year, warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Trump's remarks are the first indication of whether Nvidia's Huang knew about the woman's alleged ties to Chinese espionage.

Megaspeed's office in Singapore's central business district appeared to be operational and staffed on Tuesday.

The BBC was refused entry to its floor, but spoke to a staff member by phone who said they had no comment and directed all queries to the company's PR team.

The BBC has emailed Megaspeed several times for comment.

Nvidia, co-founded by Jensen Huang, is also a major focus in the AI technology race between the US and China, with officials in Washington treating its exports to Beijing as a matter of national security - a key reason why Huang's affair has sparked concerns.

Also on Monday, Huang and Nvidia were sued in a proposed class action lawsuit in California that accuses them of defrauding shareholders by concealing his ties with the suspected Chinese spy.

The lawsuit alleges that the company lied to the media about Jensen Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, "who is suspected of seeking to help smuggle Nvidia products to China."

The BBC has contacted Nvidia for comment on the lawsuit.

At the White House, Trump was asked several times when he was made aware of the relationship. He said he was informed "over a period of time" but was not specific.

"I hope there's no problem, I believe he is suffering greatly," the president added.

He said he spoke to Huang on the phone on Monday "just to see if he's feeling alright, how you doing and I asked him about that and he said he absolutely had no idea that the person in question was a spy".

Trump has raised concerns that allowing China to lead in AI would supercharge Beijing's military and surveillance capabilities.

The president added he was "sure" Chinese leader Xi Jinping would "ask me about it" when they next met.

Some workers the BBC spoke to at Nvidia's Santa Clara headquarters on Monday said it was business as usual, despite the intense attention on the company.

Nvidia has been around for decades, with Huang founding it with two other engineers in 1993, but its rise to one of the world's most valuable and powerful companies has only been recent.

It originally designed computer chips for gaming, but its decision to shift focus to AI development turned it into the powerhouse it is today.

Its chips have become so valuable to the AI buildout that the White House previously imposed controls on where its advanced products could be sold.

The H200, Nvidia's second most advanced semiconductor, had previously been restricted over concerns that it would give China's technology industry an edge over the US.

But Huang has long been against restricting sales to China, arguing that it would be better for the global rollout of AI to be powered by US technology.

In January, the Trump administration said it would allow the company to sell its H200 chips to Chinese customers under certain conditions.

Nvidia's most advanced AI semiconductors including the GB200 Blackwell super chip remain blocked from the Chinese market.

Additional reporting by Tessa Wong in Singapore

TechnologyTab.title: Faisal Islam: What the boss of US tech giant Nvidia told me about China and national security
TechnologyTab.text:
Jensen Huang has the air of the late Steve Jobs about him. I have interviewed both, and the up-close charisma - and occasionally scratchy genius - is shared.

Both sported a signature item of black clothing, although Huang opts for a leather jacket rather than the Apple founder's turtle neck.

Both are innovators revered in the tech world. However, Huang is now being investigated over an affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

Everything you have heard about Artificial Intelligence (AI) over the past few months - good, bad, revolutionary and catastrophic - is dependent on having the most powerful frontier AI models.

In turn they depend on the most powerful microchips, and for years that has been this very company, Nvidia, led by Huang, and his technology rooted in repurposed games graphics and the manufacturing prowess of Taiwan.

Names such as Gracehopper, Vera and Rubin mean almost nothing to the public, but are the names of chips powering the creation of AI models transforming the world.

I met Huang as he held court with reporters and offered words of encouragement for the UK's tech future during US President Donald Trump's state visit to the UK in September last year.

It was also right in the middle of his attempts to get Trump to lift export bans to China of some of the highest performing AI chips, specifically the H200.

An export ban on a less powerful chip had already been lifted. He was, I suggested to him, one of the few people who could walk into the White House to meet Trump, and a few days later meet President Xi Jinping in Beijing.

He made no secret of his views, nor his assessment that he had persuaded Trump of his case.

"President Trump is very clear. He wants America to win and and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them too. And the reason for that is because it's not a zero-sum game. The advance of human society is not a zero-sum game."

He is probably the only person in the world that could have spoken that sentence with the authority that he might have heard personally from both these superpower leaders.

However, his view about "zero-sum game" is not backed by many in national security circles.

Their view is that the race to the most advanced forms of AI is entirely zero sum, and requires the West - and the US in particular - to take critical action to hold back Chinese advancement.

The country that creates the most powerful AI systems, from the most powerful chips, will win, in terms of scientific development, of cracking encryption, economic growth and cyber-weapons.

He made a further argument: Far from being a national security challenge, it was, in fact, better for the US that the world "including China" became dependent on US systems, what they called the "American tech stack", with Nvidia chips at its core.

Huang then went even further than that, saying that President Trump "is very clear-eyed" about the idea that "this computing technology is not a national security concern".

He told me "any military is smart enough to build their military on top of their own indigenous technology, and not rely on an adversary to build their technology, build their military capability".

What does this show us?

At that time, which is the same moment now being independently investigated over national security concerns and alleged Chinese espionage, Huang was making clear public arguments to lift export bans, and seemed to have a clear idea of President Trump's views.

More than that, he was also disputing the idea that his technology, in China's hands, was any type of national security concern.

Nvidia is the absolute epicentre of the AI tech boom in the US and of the global race for AI supremacy.

Even if the boom turned to bust, Nvidia is still expected to remain in rude health.

It has actual hard revenues of about $400bn this year. Monday's drop of about 4% of its value reflects new and extraordinary risks at this junction of tech and global politics, but the chipmaker is still worth more than $4 trillion.

TechnologyTab.title: Nvidia shares tumble over investigation into Huang's affair with alleged Chinese spy
TechnologyTab.text:
Hundreds of billions of dollars have been wiped off the value of Nvidia after the US chipmaker announced an independent investigation would be carried out into its chief executive's affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

The tech firm saw its shares fall by about 4% by close of trade on Monday after Jensen Huang admitted having an extramarital affair.

Nvidia's probe came after reports that the US believed the Nvidia boss had been targeted in an espionage campaign by China.

However, China has rejected the claims, with its foreign ministry saying allegations about Chinese spies were "entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China".

Nvidia said it had no reason to believe the company's secrets or national security were compromised, but a statement by the firm's board of directors said it would begin an investigation in "light of recent reporting that founder and chief executive Jensen Huang has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort".

US intelligence officials believe Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report, external.

The report said Secretary of State Marco Rubio sent a memo to top officials in Washington last spring warning that the Nvidia boss was in a close relationship with a Chinese spy.

Alice Huang was managing director of Singaporean company Megaspeed, which has had dealings with Nvidia.

Jensen Huang admitted he was "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children. He added he was "committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America's national security" and would cooperate with the investigation.

The Nvidia co-founder has also been requested to appear for a joint closed-door briefing for several Congressional committees next week.

Members of the US House Foreign Affairs Committee last week asked Jensen Huang to appear for a closed-door briefing on his interactions with Alice Huang, as well as Nvidia's security protocols around espionage.

"Recent reports raise significant national security concerns regarding the PRC's [China's] access to sensitive US technology and information," congressmen Brian Mast, John Moolenaar, and Rick Crawford wrote in a letter.

"It is vital that Congress determines the extent to which US national security has been placed at risk."

After Nvidia's investigation was announced, other big tech bosses, including Elon Musk, came out in support of Jensen Huang to continue leading the firm.

US President Donald Trump said the Nvidia boss was an "honourable guy".

However, the news sparked a sell-off in Nvidia's shares, with about $250bn (£190bn) wiped of the company's market value.

TechnologyTab.title: Zoe Kleinman: Nvidia CEO's affair will cause ripples across US and beyond
TechnologyTab.text:
The tech world has spent the day digesting the extraordinary news that Jensen Huang - the charismatic, leather-jacket wearing chief executive of the multi-trillion dollar firm Nvidia - is being investigated by his own company over an extramarital affair with a woman alleged to be a Chinese spy.

None of us had that on our bingo cards for 2026.

Huang's alleged romantic affair with Alice Huang (no relation), the former CEO of a Singapore-based data centre company, has cast ripples far beyond his immediate family - undoubtedly on an emotional rollercoaster of their own - taking us to a crossroads at which technology, geopolitics and national security intersect.

In a nutshell, this is about the bitter rivalry between the US and China, as well as whether Jensen Huang has betrayed the US as well as his wife.

The US is locked in a fierce race with China to develop the best AI models.

"Whoever wins AI, wins," as US President Donald Trump puts it. He thinks that the country with the more dominant AI technology will benefit the most from it and, ultimately, will be the most powerful in the world. He may well be right.

Nvidia happens to make the best chips in the business for AI – so much so that it has been overwhelmed with demand.

It sets its prices accordingly: a single unit of the firm's latest kit for data centres starts at £37,000 ($50,000). A medium or large site might have hundreds of them.

The US administration initially slapped an export ban on Nvidia's more recent devices to prevent China from taking advantage of their superior capabilities. It has since softened the rules a little.

But there are suggestions that Alice Huang's company, Megaspeed, may have been involved in sneaking them into the country while she was in charge. Bloomberg reported that the firm bought billions of dollars worth of Nvidia tech in November 2025. Megaspeed denies that it was used illegitimately.

For his part, Jensen Huang has lobbied heavily for the export rules between the two countries to be relaxed, arguing against the weight of general opinion that the AI race doesn't matter and that it would be no bad thing for China to become dependent on US tech.

"President Trump wants American to win and President Xi wants China to win, and it's possible for both of them to do so," he told the BBC last year.

I think it's safe to assume that neither country sees it that way.

The difficult questions Nvidia now has to try to answer include whether Alice gained special access to the firm's latest technology, either deliberately or not, via Jensen - and, if so, whether she shared it with Beijing or others.

We don't know when their affair began or ended, but there are numerous photos and videos of Jensen and Alice together at events. It is feasible that there were moments when they spent quite a lot of time together and Jensen has talked about always having an eye on his work.

China denies that she was engaged in espionage.

Interest in economic espionage is neither new nor unique to China. But many Western countries say that China does it on a grand scale, using a combination of technology tools and agents embedded in various organisations - including private companies.

China having access to significant enough numbers of Nvidia's chips to make use of them, or stripping them down and learning how to make its own versions, would infuriate the Trump administration, which is trying to keep its AI technology close to its chest.

Some models have even been withheld from the UK-based AI Safety Institute on the grounds that they are potentially too dangerous to be shared. The US does not want anyone having a headstart or misusing its innovations.

Another potential bombshell lies in the form of any national security information to which Jensen Huang may have been privy.

He is a man operating at the very top of the US elite - one of a handful of people who could probably walk into the White House unannounced and have tea with Trump. He has influence, he has access and he has powerful friends. It's quite possible that secrets were shared with him.

Nvidia says there's no evidence so far that he passed anything on and the firm has launched an internal investigation. Huang says he will co-operate and wants to keep his job - though if nothing else, he has broken Nvidia's own code of conduct, which states that company members should not have relationships with clients.

But can he survive?

At present, he has the backing of both the Nvidia board and Trump, who described him as "honourable" and speculated that there must have been a reason for what had transpired. In other words, he's not throwing his tech boss buddy under the bus.

Nvidia's share price has fallen but has not tanked spectacularly, suggesting shareholders are not abandoning the company under his stewardship in their droves either.

An AI industry with a weakened Nvidia would undoubtedly be a slower one.

And there isn't really a natural successor waiting in the wings to replace Jensen were he forced out.

Huang has run Nvidia for more than 30 years - to many, he is Nvidia. He has steered it through multiple crises and it was his decision for the firm to focus on AI before it was trendy.

He is known to be a demanding boss who expects staff to work long hours and to high standards. There are stories about him calling all-staff meetings to tell off individuals who had made mistakes. He has said this was to prevent others making the same errors – but you can only imagine how it felt for those on the receiving end.

While he awaits the conclusion of the investigation into his actions, Huang must hope that, despite not tolerating the mistakes of his colleagues in the past, they will be gracious about his own failings.

And he must also live with the irony that he was potentially caught out not by a sophisticated high-tech sting, but by the oldest trick in the book: a honey trap.

TechnologyTab.title: Australia considers criminal penalties for rogue AI in wake of OpenAI hack
TechnologyTab.text:
Australia plans to create a new AI safety regulator and has flagged criminal penalties for tech companies who do not comply, months after an OpenAI hack.

In September, Australia's Prime Minister Anthony Albanese revealed that a rogue OpenAI agent had "infiltrated" a government health website and other systems, and criticised the company for taking months to tell them about the hack.

On Tuesday, he released the 18 recommendations made after a "rapid review" into the breaches including new safety and security standards for AI companies such as mandatory reporting of hacks.

AI brings opportunities, he said, but Australia must prepare for the "new risks" from this "rapidly advancing technology".

"The law needs to get ahead of and, in some cases, make sure that it catches up with, what is a very fast changing world," Albanese said.

One of the recommendations suggests changes to criminal law to have a standalone "failure to prevent" offence .

This would criminalise instances where a company develops "an AI model that engages in harmful conduct" and "fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm".

The review also recommended "mandatory, time-bound AI safety reporting" of hacks.

This point addresses what Albanese had earlier called his "disappointment" in the months-long delay for OpenAI to tell his government about the breach.

In June, a statistics portal containing "non-sensitive" data from Australia's universal healthcare scheme Medicare was hacked by a rogue OpenAI agent.

OpenAI said it only learnt of the breach in August while reviewing "misaligned model activity" and emailed a general inbox of an Australian government agency on 10 September.

It took several more days before the email was escalated to Australia's cybersecurity centre, with a message then sent to a government minister ahead of the prime minister being told.

Albanese said he spoke to OpenAI boss Sam Altman and raised "Australia's extreme concern about this incident", with Altman acknowledging there were "issues with protocols" at OpenAI.

Days after the hacks were revealed, OpenAI delayed its rollout of a new AI model, citing safety concerns.

TechnologyTab.title: Jensen Huang: What we know about Nvidia CEO's affair with suspected Chinese spy
TechnologyTab.text:
One of the Artificial Intelligence (AI) industry's most important figures has been accused of having an affair with a suspected Chinese spy, prompting an investigation.

US intelligence officials believed that Chinese businesswoman Alice Huang, who had a close relationship with Nvidia CEO and co-founder Jensen Huang, was a spy for Beijing, according to a New York Times report.

On Sunday, Huang admitted, external to having been "unfaithful" to his wife and apologised for hurting her and their children.

US tech giant Nvidia, one of the most valuable companies in the world, has opened an independent investigation into the reports. The firm said it does not believe US national security had been compromised - and added that Huang was committed to continuing to lead the company.

President Donald Trump said on Monday that the FBI is also investigating the affair.

The FBI declined to comment further when contacted by the BBC.

Trump said he spoke with Huang on Monday following reports that the US believed he had been targeted in a Chinese espionage campaign.

"I asked him that question, 'Did you have any idea she was a spy?' He said 'I had no idea she was a spy' and I really believe him," Trump told reporters.

Here is what we know about the affair and why it matters.

US officials believed that Alice Huang had been recruited to spy by China's top intelligence agency, the New York Times reported, external. Her current whereabouts are unknown.

Alice Huang, who is of no relation to Jensen Huang, was a top executive at Singapore-based data centre firm Megaspeed between March and November 2023. The firm had been suspected of helping divert Nvidia chips to China, a concern that Nvidia maintains was investigated and debunked.

However, Megaspeed is under investigation by the Singapore government regarding previous allegations that the company was circumventing US sanctions on the export of Nvidia's high-end chips. The BBC has contacted Megaspeed for comment.

The company told the New York Times last month its current leadership took the allegations seriously and had appointed external legal advisers to conduct an internal investigation.

Surveillance reportedly revealed communications between Alice Huang and an American citizen, who was subsequently identified as Jensen Huang through a process known as "unmasking".

It remains unclear what, if any, intelligence Alice Huang – who is also known as Huang Le – allegedly gathered and passed to Beijing. She did not respond to the paper's request for comment.

When the BBC asked Nvidia if the company was aware of intelligence concerns, the company said it was not.

"We trust that if we were the target of a genuine threat, the US government would have notified us," an Nvidia spokesperson told the BBC.

China has rejected the spying allegations.

Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun told reporters on Monday at a regular daily press briefing: "We have already responded to this. The allegations about Chinese spies are entirely groundless, speculative and intended to smear and malign China."

The New York Times reported in late October that Trump had been briefed last year on intelligence alleging Alice Huang was spying on China's behalf.

Asked by reporters on Sunday whether he wished he had "acted on the intelligence", Trump responded: "No, I don't think so. I think he's an honourable guy."

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, meanwhile, refused to comment when asked about Huang. Last spring, the secretary of state reportedly oversaw the drafting of a memo that warned the Trump administration about Huang's relationship with the Chinese businesswoman, according to the New York Times.

Nvidia is at the heart of US and China's AI race, which is why the billionaire's affair has sparked national security fears among American lawmakers.

Trump has said "whoever wins AI wins", and the fear is that if China gains the upper hand in AI, it will supercharge the country's military and surveillance capabilities.

The US advantage is in large part because of US companies like Nvidia, working with producers like the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which makes more than 90% of the world's most advanced chips.

Since 2022, the US has used various export controls to keep the top tech out of China, which it says helps retain America's competitive edge and protects its national security.

This means companies like Nvidia have been largely locked out of the world's most lucrative market, with Huang once saying that Nvidia's share of the Chinese market had gone from around 95% to effectively zero.

Huang has engaged in shuttle diplomacy between Washington and Beijing, hoping to find a US-approved way back in, and shaping US policy on China along the way.

Sunday's revelations may explain why Huang has failed to bring home the biggest prize of all to Nvidia: the Trump administration's blessing to sell all but its most advanced chips to China.

Born in Taiwan in 1963, Huang was nine years old when his family moved to the West Coast of the US. He graduated as an electrical engineer from Oregon State University, and then with a master's degree in the same field from Stanford University.

Huang then worked at US chip firm AMD before co-founding Nvidia. Known as "Daddy Huang" in Taiwan and once lauded as the "Taylor Swift of tech", he has a reputation as a workaholic and perfectionist with incredibly high standards for his staff.

He has an estimated fortune of $155bn (£115bn), according to the Bloomberg Billionaires Index.

"Jensen Huang is a tech visionary of the likes of Steve Jobs," Stephen Witt, the author of Thinking Machine, a biography on Huang, told the BBC, adding that he was responsible for creating AI hardware as we know it today.

Huang has a famously close relationship with Trump. At the recent AI summit at the White House, where 42 tech executives were present, the president was flanked by Elon Musk and Huang.

Trump said he had not spoken to the Nvidia boss since news of the investigation emerged.

"I just know he's a fine person, but you never know what's going on," Trump told reporters, adding that he had "done an amazing job for our country".

Founded by Huang and fellow electrical engineers Chris Malachowsky and Curtis Priem in 1993, the company was originally known for chips that process graphics, particularly for computer games.

Eventually it changed focus to AI, a field it now dominates.

Huang rescued Nvidia from bankruptcy on more than one occasion, and took risks on AI a long time before the rest of the world did, effectively building the infrastructure from scratch.

"Today when we think of that, we think of these giant data centres - none of that existed. There were no customers for the stuff he was building. In fact his first customer was Open AI at the time they had 30 people - he actually gave it to them, he donated it to them," Witt told the BBC.

Every notable tech company building AI tools and infrastructure, including Amazon, Meta, Google, and Microsoft, now use Nvidia chips.

Currently worth $4.5tn (£3.4tn), Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies ever.

For now, the firm's board appears to have little appetite for removing Huang, saying in a statement on Sunday that they have "confidence in Jensen and his leadership team".

Sources tell the BBC his removal is unlikely because there is so much money at stake.

There is no public succession plan for the 63-year-old. He has often said he hopes to continue in the role for decades, and Bloomberg reports he has created an informal leadership structure around him unlike a traditional company's hierarchy.

His children, Spencer and Madison, and son-in-law Nico Caprez work at Nvidia in senior roles.

Huang met his future wife Lori Mills at Oregon State University while studying electrical engineering in the early 1980s. The pair were lab partners.

They married in 1985, about eight years before he co-founded Nvidia, and have two children, Madison and Spencer.

In 2007, the couple founded the Jen-Hsun and Lori Huang Foundation. The charitable fund has seen its assets surge in recent years, driven by the soaring value of Nvidia shares, and is estimated to be worth more than $9bn.

Its donations include tens of millions of dollars to engineering programmes at Oregon State and Stanford University.

Witt told the BBC that Huang has gone to great lengths to present himself as a family man, adding: "That's very important to him".

"He praises his wife, he talks about her in very glowing ways," he added. "The fallout of this would be bad for anyone's family. But for someone who has gone to such great lengths to cultivate an image of being a family guy and who keeps his children very close, it is very bad."

Additional reporting by Tom McArthur in London, Ayeshea Perera and Tessa Wong in Singapore and Helen Davidson in Sydney

TechnologyTab.title: Vinted and eBay could be included in under-16 social media ban, minister says
TechnologyTab.text:
Vinted and eBay could be included in the list of platforms set to be banned for children aged under 16, the culture secretary has said.

Lisa Nandy said the government was "looking seriously" at including the retailing websites in the social media ban "to keep children safe".

The UK's social media ban for under-16s is set to come into force in March next year, with children barred from accessing platforms such as Instagram, TikTok and Snapchat.

In response, eBay said it was looking forward to "understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government". Vinted said it welcomed "open dialogue" with ministers and the regulator on the issue.

Asked on the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme whether the government was looking to ban under-16s from Vinted and eBay, Nandy said: "We are looking seriously at doing so in order to keep children safe."

It came after the Sunday Times reported, external that the UK's social media ban was being expanded to include the popular second-hand online marketplaces.

The move was due to fears that messaging functions on the platforms allowed strangers to groom children, according to the newspaper. It suggested similar reselling platforms, Depop and Facebook Marketplace, would also be included in the list of banned sites.

Businesses and individuals sell a host of goods on eBay, which has been a major global player in the online reselling market for years. The platform states on its website that it currently requires all of its members to be over 18 years old because listings involve "entering into a contract".

Vinted is aimed at over 18s, but its terms and conditions do allow parents or guardians to create accounts for their children, which must be used under parental supervision.

The site, on which users mostly buy and sell unwanted clothes and other fashion items, has grown rapidly recently to reach 17 million UK users.

A Vinted spokesperson said direct messaging was "part of how the platform works" but that it had a "zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content" and had moderation teams and tools to spot and remove "activity that breaks our rules".

"When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities," they said.

An eBay spokesperson said the company was "focused on providing a trusted and safe marketplace experience for our millions of customers".

"While the details of the proposed legislation are not yet clear, we look forward to understanding more and continuing to work constructively with the government," they added.

The government announced it would ban under-16s accessing social media in June this year, with children prevented from accessing 10 of the biggest platforms.

YouTube will also be banned for under-16s, but YouTube Kids - a version of the video-sharing app designed to be safe for children - will not be included in the measures.

A complete list of affected platforms has not yet been released, but the government said it would cover those "whose purpose is to enable social interaction and which allow users to post material".

That means platforms that have livestreaming or features that enable the potential for strangers to contact children will also be restricted, which includes gaming sites.

It does not mean that Roblox, the biggest gaming site in the UK for those aged eight to 12, for example, will be banned for under-16s. However, certain features such as its chat function will be restricted.

But Matthew Sinclair, a senior director at the Computer and Communications Industry Association, which represents tech companies, argued that ministers should prevent the rules having "scope creep".

He said a restriction on messaging for under-16s "would not stop at social media and would reach into the services families depend on to stay in touch", and urged the government to "ensure any new restrictions are proportionate and effective."

The UK's ban comes after a similar one was introduced in Australia last year.

Many children there have found ways to get round it, but the UK has said it intends to take a tougher approach.

In recent weeks, attention has turned to how a social media ban would be enforced.

Last month, the communications regulator Ofcom set out its recommendations for the most effective ways to identify which of the UK's millions of social media users are aged over 16.

Rani Govender, head of online child safety at the NSPCC, said the "real question" going forward was how the government ensured age checks were effective.

"But effective age checks are only part of the solution," she added. "Tech companies must also be required to build child safety into every platform, device and AI tool, so children are protected from harmful and illegal content and only able to access age-appropriate services."
