articles.title: Ocarina of Time review: Does Nintendo's Zelda remake match its original?
articles.text:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time was finally released on Thursday, after years of rumours that Nintendo would remake the game - considered one of the best ever made.

IGN called it "the biggest game of the decade" in their review, external when it launched in 1998 on the N64, and it set the standard for 3D games.

A lot of the things we take for granted in modern games - such as riding a horse, fighting with a sword and shield, or locking on to enemies with the tap of a button - were pioneered or perfected in Ocarina of Time.

It received an almost perfect score from critics and, decades on, remains the highest-rated game in history on Metacritic, which aggregates reviews.

So how do you remake what many consider a masterpiece?

Those like me who grew up playing the original will feel right at home here.

Nintendo has decided against reinventing the wheel, instead producing something which plays very similarly to the N64 classic.

As I've said before, video game remakes are a bit different to film or TV - gaming fans often clamour for a new take on their favourites, hoping developers harness evolution in tech to make them fresh.

And games have come a long way in the almost 30 years since the original Ocarina of Time came out.

"When you compare the games in the past and the games in modern times, so to speak, the norms of what people expect from a game have evolved naturally," Nintendo producer Hidemaro Fujibayashi told me.

"In the past, games where the users may have needed more imagination to fill the blanks or the gaps are now clearly expressed through the graphics that they see on the screen."

But fancy graphics have come at a price - a pivot away from realism into something a bit more cartoonish. Some might even be disappointed by this, given the N64 game had quite horrifying elements in places.

One was the Skulltula House, a room where people had been morphed into human-spider hybrids.

"Back when we created the original Ocarina of Time, the means to convey or express ideas was limited compared with what we have now," series producer Eiji Aonuma - who worked on the original game - said.

"With regard to even the so-called scary elements, we strove to add a touch of the comical."

But he told the BBC that enhanced graphics and lighting capabilities unintentionally exaggerated the already-spooky Skulltula House and its potential to strike fear into players.

"When we carried out the test play, the testers were telling us, 'Oh, this is too scary'," he said. "So of course, in the end product, we've made the necessary adjustments so that we can retain the same balance that we had achieved in the original."

I spoke to a few YouTubers about the upcoming game to get their thoughts - and the response was overwhelmingly positive.

Mike Channell, co-editor of the YouTube channel Outside Xbox, said he believed the remake had been made "very meticulously" in the hopes of living up to fan expectations.

"Having played the game, it's clear that serious thought has gone into every decision, to the point where I'm not convinced this remake has taken any less time and effort than an all-new Zelda game," he said.

"Ocarina of Time is obviously one of the great video game experiences in the history of the medium, but I have no doubt this new version will be the best way to experience this story.

"It's fleshed out as a world, sumptuously detailed, and the controls match 21st-Century expectations."

Ed King, known as Zeltik to his 893,000 followers on YouTube, said "the level of detail and charm" in the Ocarina of Time remake stood out.

"The Forest Temple has always been my favourite Zelda dungeon: a mysterious, haunted mansion in the deep woods, a lost work of man slowly being reclaimed by nature," he said. "The remake really leans into the surreal, uncanny nature of the original dungeon."

And fellow YouTuber StrawHatMidas said it was the "perfect" way to "bring this classic back".

"Not only does the game pay homage to the Nintendo 64 original, but it also expands on the things that made it so memorable," he said. "Everything from the world and atmosphere to the controls and soundtrack feels like a love letter to the classic Zelda formula."

Nintendo has made some big changes, not least to the Water Temple - a dungeon about two thirds into the game.

Aonuma said, having worked on the original, this was what he personally wanted to change most due to its reputation for being "very, very difficult".

He said there was now "a greater facility in tackling" the dungeon, as players can now easily change a critical in-game item known as heavy boots and have "the ability to leverage the camera orientation".

I grew up playing Zelda on the N64, which pioneered the joystick - but nowadays two sticks is the standard, with one to move and one to control the camera.

As far as I'm concerned, being able to freely move the camera this time round was a significant improvement.

At times, the trip down memory lane was captivating. I knew where to go and what to do, thanks to a kind of muscle memory. However, on occasion that took away from the experience - with some tasks achieved too easily and some puzzles too quickly because I recalled their solutions.

Some people will love how similar it is, but I have to wonder if Nintendo has played things a bit too safe.

I don't think the developers see it that way.

"Even if the game may look different, we've maintained the essence that the original developers wanted to and hopefully conveyed through the original Ocarina of Time," Fujibayashi said.

Don't get me wrong - the game has lots of changes and surprises, and I won't spoil them, but I wish there had been more.

Then again, perhaps the best games leave you wanting more.

Or as Mike put it: "I loved the original as much as the next person, but I don't think I'll be going back to it."

Fans will no doubt wonder whether this is it, or if there will be more Zelda on the horizon. With the franchise's first movie coming next year, there's certainly more to come in the short term.

And in the long term, I wondered if with 30 more years of technological advancements, Nintendo might consider remaking the game once again.

"I will be long retired," Aonuma said, with a laugh.

articles.title: Elon Musk appears to signal the end of the road for Cybertruck
articles.text:
Tesla will wind down production of its Cybertruck vehicles at its Texas factory next year, Elon Musk says.

He did not spell out whether it plans to stop making them entirely or shift production elsewhere, but did say the decision was to "make room" for building more of its self-driving Cybercab cars.

But the project's lead engineer, Wes Morrill, appeared to suggest the vehicle was being discontinued, writing on X: "Cybertruck was an incredible technology development platform and lives on through Cybercab."

With its distinctive angular looks, the Cybertruck attracted diehard fans, but was beset by delays before being launched in 2023 and has had disappointing sales numbers since.

Tesla fans have been mourning the news online, with one person calling it "the best vehicle Tesla has ever made, external" as he lamented it being "discontinued next year".

Musk responded to the user, external with the word "true", adding: "But the Cybertruck fleet will be around for a long time."

Tesla's stock rose 4.7% on Friday after his announcement.

The vehicle has always been a passion project for Musk. He said it was "way more awesome than people realise, external" in March, and called it the "best product Tesla has ever made to date, external" in April.

But there have always been big questions about whether consumers shared that view and whether the Cybertruck could cut through and earn a spot in the US' lucrative truck market.

It was not helped by inauspicious introduction to the public in 2019 when Musk attempted to show off the Cybertruck's apparently unbreakable glass, only for it to shatter during a live demonstration.

articles.title: Nvidia and Jensen Huang sued in US over affair with alleged Chinese spy
articles.text:
Nvidia and its chief executive, Jensen Huang, have been accused of misleading shareholders in a lawsuit over the Chinese spying scandal engulfing the $4.3tn (£3.2tn) company.

The legal action came as Donald Trump said the FBI was investigating Huang’s affair with an alleged Chinese spy.

According to a complaint filed in federal court in ​California, Nvidia and Huang misled shareholders in connection with the executive’s alleged ​affair with Alice Huang, a former executive of Singapore-based ⁠Megaspeed, who is not related to him.

The lawsuit claims both parties did ​not disclose that the matter raised national security concerns that threatened the chipmaker’s reputation and business prospects.

The New York Times reported on the alleged relationship last month, and said US authorities had concluded Alice Huang ​was a Chinese intelligence asset.

Nvidia described its executive’s interaction with Alice Huang as “not unusual or unexpected” in a comment submitted to the New York Times last month, adding that “meetings with customers are part of a CEO’s job; Jensen talks with thousands of customer executives every year”.

On Sunday, Huang admitted he had been “unfaithful” to his wife, without identifying the person involved in the affair.

The lawsuit claims the NYT statement was “materially false and misleading at the time it was made because Jensen Huang had an affair with Alice Huang.”

It also accused the company of making false and misleading statements about its relationship with Megaspeed, which has reportedly been investigated over suspicions that it may have been diverting Nvidia chips to China in contravention of US export restrictions.

Huang said in an interview published on 30 October that “we’ve studied all their [Megaspeed] deployments of our GPUs and counted every one”. He added: “And I think the US government also has as well.”

In a statement last year Megaspeed said it has acted “fully in compliance with all applicable laws, including US export control regulations”.

Nvidia announced on Sunday it was conducting an independent investigation into reports that Huang was the “target of a foreign intelligence effort”. Shares in the company fell on Monday, closing down 4.3%, reducing Nvidia’s ​market ⁠value by approximately $190bn. The lawsuit was filed five minutes after the US stock market closed.

Nvidia and Megaspeed did not immediately respond to ​a request for comment on the lawsuit.

Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993 and has led the California company as it became the world’s most valuable chipmaker and made him ​one of the ​world’s most ⁠prominent symbols of the artificial intelligence boom.

It is common for shareholders to ⁠sue ​companies after unexpected share price declines. ​Nvidia shareholders, led by Mark Kistenmacher, a retail investor, are seeking unspecified damages from the defendants in the class action suit, the term for a legal action where a person or small group of people sues an entity on behalf of a larger group.

Several US law firms have announced investigations into whether Nvidia misled investors and have asked shareholders to get in touch.

Trump said on Monday that the FBI is investigating Huang’s affair but said he did not think the executive had a reason to worry.

“I know the FBI is looking into it in terms of something else, and I think that he’ll be in good shape,” Trump said at a White House briefing.

“I did speak to him today just to see if he’s feeling all right, how you’re doing,” Trump said. “He said he had absolutely no idea that the person in question was a spy.”

Huang said in an open letter posted on Nvidia’s website: “I support the investigation and will cooperate fully. I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security,”

Reuters contributed to this report

The AI doomsday threat: Distinguishing facts from fear

On Monday 30 November, join Dan Milmo, Prof Dame Wendy Hall and Stuart J Russel as they discuss the warnings surrounding artificial intelligence and how we can separate fact from speculation. Livestreamed only.

articles.title: UK social media ban expansion for under-16s could cover YouTube Kids
articles.text:
A substantial expansion of the social media ban for under-16s could inadvertently lead to a ban on YouTube Kids and other sites that had been thought exempt, sources briefed on the government’s proposals have said.

One source close to the talks said the regulations now under consideration meant up to 150 platforms, including games platforms such as Lego Play, could be covered by the ban, which is set to come into force in March.

The regulations will be sent for cabinet signoff this week, and the culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, is expected to lay them in parliament in December.

Ministers are understood to be keen for a catch-all approach that limits ban workarounds. Critics of Australia’s social media prohibition say teenagers have switched to new platforms or found innovative ways of messaging using other seemingly innocuous sites.

Tech companies, industry groups and MPs have been briefed that the government’s working proposal focuses on recommender systems and user-generated content.

Spotify – which has some user-generated content and shows recommended music or podcasts – could technically be in scope if those proposals are enacted, though the music streaming site has sought reassurances that it would not face a ban because it is not primarily a social platform.

One industry source said: “We all share the goal of keeping teenagers safe online. Proposals have to be workable, and a situation where eBay, Lego, YouTube Kids and Spotify aren’t clear whether they comply is unsustainable. Detailed guidelines can’t come soon enough.”

Another said: “The whole internet has a recommender system. The regulation is just too broad. But they want to make it really broad and legally airtight so they can be prepared for any eventuality.”

Companies are expected to be briefed on the final proposal in the coming days by the Department for Culture, Media and Sport (DCMS) and No 10.

When the ban was announced by Keir Starmer in June, the government said it would ensure the ban did not include educational services, e-commerce platforms or music streaming, saying there would be “a narrowly defined list of exemptions to the definitions which will be kept under review”.

But tech companies are understood to be telling the government that removing the recommender algorithm would make it impossible for their sites to function.

The regulations do not require primary legislation in the House of Commons, and will be tabled as an addition to the Children’s Wellbeing and Schools Act.

Ministers are also looking at a second tranche of regulations in the spring which could cover e-commerce platforms such as Vinted, eBay and Depop. MPs and campaigners have raised concerns with Nandy that teenagers and groomers can find innovative ways to communicate on platforms that allow unknown or anonymous user messaging, such as those websites.

After Nandy confirmed in interviews on Sunday that the government was looking to bring Vinted and other e-commerce platforms in scope, officials held a panicked call with retailers on Tuesday where several are understood to have strongly contested the plans.

Another industry figure said it would be illogical for the government to continue to allow messaging apps such as WhatsApp and iMessage – but ban platforms such as Vinted and eBay because they had messaging capabilities.

The minister for online safety, Ian Murray, also confirmed to MPs last week that the government was looking at those sites for the next tranche of regulations which examines “features and functions” and is expected next spring.

“Platforms that might have been out of scope are perhaps being brought into scope by having new functionalities that we might think are different from the social media platforms we are seeking to regulate. For example, Spotify has introduced stranger conversation functionality to its platform,” he said.

Murray told MPs that platforms which redesigned their services to remove harmful or addictive functions would have a route to removing themselves from the banned list.

“The way back is to comply with the regulations and fall out of scope. That is an easy thing to say but not an easy thing to deliver, but that is the principle with which we will go forward on this,” he said.

He said platforms such as YouTube Kids and Lego Play would need to demonstrate they did not have harmful algorithms.

“Are there ways in which you can stop the harms being created by the algorithms, the recommender systems, the commenting systems or the conversations that can be had with strangers?

“If you have created a service that complies with all the regulations, is it then available to under-16s? I would say that, currently, the government’s position is that, yes, there has to be an off ramp.”

Tech industry bodies have told the government that platforms such as YouTube Kids cease to function without the recommender system, making it impossible for them to comply with the “off ramp”.

DCMS has been approached to comment.

articles.title: Anthropic targets valuation of up to $1.4tn in stock market flotation
articles.text:
Anthropic is seeking a valuation of up to $1.4tn (£1.1tn) in its imminent stock market flotation, short of the $2tn that had been expected before investors started to question the durability of the AI boom.

The developer of the Claude chatbot was widely reported to be targeting a $2tn initial public offering on Wall Street but its sights have been set lower, according to a US regulatory filing on Tuesday.

Anthropic is aiming to raise up to $64.4bn by selling 825m shares in the IPO priced up to $78 a share. The California-based company will also raise a further $26bn via a separate private placement deal ⁠with cornerstone investors including the Google parent, Alphabet, and the chipmaker Nvidia.

An extra $9.7bn could be raised from a so-called greenshoe offering, which kicks in if investor demand is high and would take the total amount raised by Anthropic to approximately $100bn if the shares sold at the top end of the price range.

At the upper bracket of the $70-$78 per share price range, Anthropic would be worth $1.4tn on a fully diluted basis – which means taking into account all the common shares in the company in existence, including employee stock options.

Trading in Anthropic shares is expected to begin next week.

Investor jitters over the AI boom were crystallised last week when the US midterm elections produced victories for datacentre opponents. This has added to already existing concerns, such as how quickly – or if at all – companies can generate a return on their spending on AI infrastructure.

Brian Hopkins, a principal analyst at Forrester Research, said the midterm elections gave investors the chance to correct valuations that they were beginning to have concerns about, because of worries about the financial sustainability of the AI build-out. The election results brought those concerns to a head, Hopkins said.

“The market needed an excuse to correct itself a little bit in terms of valuations,” he said. “The US election spook is what has caused it.”

As a consequence, Anthropic’s valuation has also been lowered from an anticipated $2tn, he added.

The largest ever stock market listing is Elon Musk’s SpaceX, which joined the US stock market with a valuation of $1.78tn, raising $75bn. The company, whose assets include Musk’s rocket launch business and the X social media platform, is now worth just under $2tn.

However, the $100bn that could be raised in the Anthropic offering will exceed the amount raised by SpaceX.

Dario Amodei, Anthropic’s chief executive, is selling about $260m worth of shares in the float, as are his six fellow co-founders. At the top of the price range the co-founders’ stakes will be worth more than $18bn each.

A Chinese spying scandal enveloping Nvidia, a cornerstone company for AI investors, also threatens to overshadow the industry but has not affected share prices so far – other than Nvidia’s.

The updated Anthropic filing stated that the company’s annual revenue is now running at $81bn as of 31 October, up $10bn from the previous month.

Anthropic’s main expenditure is on the computing power, from datacentres, that is key to developing and operating its AI systems. According to its prospectus, Anthropic has compute purchase commitments and lease agreements of more than $70bn over the next 12 months and more than $450bn by 2030, with a further $450bn due by 2045.

In a podcast appearance earlier this year, Anthropic’s Amodei explained how compute commitments had to be matched by revenue growth.

“I could buy $1tn of compute that starts at the end of 2027. If my revenue is not $1tn, if it’s even $800bn, there’s no force on Earth, there’s no hedge on Earth, that could stop me from going bankrupt,” he told podcaster Dwarkesh Patel.

On Tuesday the Financial Times reported that the investment bank Goldman Sachs, which is leading the float along with Morgan Stanley, is forecasting Anthropic will generate annual revenues of $600bn by 2030.

articles.title: Who is David Walliams? His career and controversies including Little Britain and BGT
articles.text:
David Walliams has been accused of grooming young fans and harassing women in the workplace, after failing to stop the Guardian and ITN publishing claims against him.

A three-year investigation, external by the two news organisations alleged the Little Britain star and former Britain's Got Talent judge preyed on teenage girls as young as 15 and young women, external for sexual purposes.

He had sought a High Court injunction to prevent publication, with his lawyers arguing if allegations were made public Walliams would likely kill himself. The court refused the request.

Walliams has denied all of the allegations but in a letter to journalists working on the investigation acknowledged "at times I behaved thoughtlessly towards other people I had casual sexual relationships with".

He added: "I am not a sexual predator. I have not broken the law, but I am devastated that some of the women I met 10 to 20 years ago have now expressed hurt or anger towards me."

The 55-year-old became a household name in the early 2000s through Little Britain, his comedy sketch show with Matt Lucas broadcast on the BBC.

Walliams published his first children's book, The Boy in the Dress, in 2008, and his stories soon became best-sellers and led to comparisons with Roald Dahl.

His 23 children's books have sold more than 50 million copies worldwide, but he was dropped by publisher HarperCollins in 2025 after allegations of inappropriate behaviour, which he denied.

In 2012, Walliams became a judge on Britain's Got Talent, and was voted best TV judge at the National TV Awards (NTAs) four times. He was replaced as a judge in 2022.

Before entering showbusiness, Walliams was born David Williams but changed his surname's spelling to avoid having the same name as another member of entertainment union Equity.

He was married to Dutch model Lara Stone from 2010 to 2015 and they have a son.

That hasn't stopped speculation about Walliams' sexuality. He has described himself as "bi-curious" and called his 2012 autobiography Camp David – but said he isn't attracted to men in the way he is to women.

Walliams and Lucas won a string of awards for Little Britain including three Baftas and two International Emmys, and the programme was watched by 10 million people in the UK.

But in the two decades since it ended, views about the show and what is and is not acceptable to joke about have radically altered. The programme has been criticised for its use of blackface and for stereotyping and mocking characters from minority and marginalised groups.

In the wake of the Black Lives Matter movement in 2020, Little Britain was removed from streaming services including BBC iPlayer, Netflix and BritBox.

Another of the duo's shows, 2010 airport comedy Come Fly With Me, was also removed from BritBox a decade after its original broadcast, due to the show's use of racial stereotypes and using make-up to portray people from other ethnic groups.

Little Britain was restored to iPlayer in 2022 with several scenes cut out. Walliams and Lucas said they had re-edited the show to "better reflect the changes in the cultural landscape since the show was made".

Not all the criticisms of Walliams have involved new standards being applied to older work.

Walliams had to apologise after two charity performances, during which he yanked down not only the trousers but also the underwear of actor Jeremy Edwards and music producer Mark Ronson.

In 2020, he was booed while hosting the NTAs after making a joke about Caroline Flack being out of work, at a time when she had stepped down from hosting Love Island and was waiting to appear in court, having been charged for actual bodily harm following a row with her boyfriend.

Later in 2022, he was replaced as a judge on Britain's Got Talent after a Guardian story about a leaked recording of Walliams making insulting remarks about contestants during breaks from filming.

In the incident, which happened in 2020, he spoke about a pensioner to whom he had taken a strong dislike and a woman who he described as "the slightly boring girl you would meet in the pub" who "you would want to have sex with, but then decide not to". He used much stronger language when talking about both.

Walliams apologised, explaining: "These were private conversations and - like most conversations with friends - were never intended to be shared. Nevertheless, I am sorry."

He sued the show's producers Freemantle for misuse of his private information and breaching data protection laws. An "amicable resolution" was reached, with the production company apologising for the recording being made public.

Further controversy came in June 2025, when it emerged that Walliams had given two Nazi salutes during the recording of BBC One's Would I Lie to You? Christmas special.

Banijay UK, which owned the show's production company Zeppotron, apologised, adding: "It was immediately acknowledged during the recording that this segment would not be broadcast under any circumstances." Walliams has never commented on the incident.

Then in December 2025, HarperCollins, the publisher of his hugely successful children's books, announced that following a change of CEO, the company would no longer look after new releases by Walliams.

He was dropped over allegations he had harassed female members of staff, with HarperCollins explaining that the company took "employee wellbeing extremely seriously and has processes in place for reporting and investigating concerns".

The Daily Telegraph reported that an internal investigation had been opened the previous year after a complaint was made by a junior member of staff about his behaviour. This reportedly found that staff had been told to only meet Walliams in pairs and advised against going to his house.

Walliams' spokesperson responded by saying he "strongly denies that he has behaved inappropriately" and that he had "never been informed of any allegations raised against him" by the publisher.

Then in September 2026, HarperCollins doubled down by announcing that they were cutting all ties with Walliams and would no longer represent his back catalogue, meaning that when his books sold out in shops, they would not be replaced.

articles.title: Booker Prize 2026: M John Harrison's 'baffling but brilliant' novel The End of Everything wins
articles.text:
Author M John Harrison has become the oldest ever winner of the Booker Prize, picking up the prestigious literary award for his post-apocalyptic novel The End of Everything.

Harrison, 81, who has built a cult following over his 60-year career, was named the winner of the £50,000 prize at a ceremony in London on Monday.

The End of Everything is set in the years after a mysterious catastrophe that caused British society as we know it to collapse. It has divided opinion among readers, and was described as "bleak but brilliant" and "dreamlike and baffling" by one critic.

Dame Mary Beard, who chaired the Booker judges, said: "It's a challenging read, but some of the best fiction is challenging."

Dame Mary added: "It's a book that turns you upside down, raises a wry smile – and surprisingly, given the subject matter, leaves you with a twinge of optimism."

Harrison began writing in the 1960s and has published 13 novels, five short story collections and an "anti-memoir". He has now surpassed Margaret Atwood as the oldest ever Booker winner.

While he dislikes labels like science fiction and fantasy, he has been called "the titan of literary science fiction", and Booker Prize chief executive Gaby Wood said he is "the first Booker winner to have emerged from the bona fide SF world".

"He is a genuinely original thinker, a genre-defying writer who takes ideas seriously," Wood said.

"Though very unsettling, The End of Everything is not in fact a strange book. It's a realist book about a strange world, populated by desperate, unmoored characters."

The story follows a man and his aunt who must muddle through on the south-east English coast in the aftermath of an unexplained disaster and the arrival of mysterious alien beings.

The author has said he deliberately omitted as much explanation about the background to the events as possible, in order to make readers feel the same disorientation as the characters.

He has said: "The End of Everything is about trying to live as if nothing has gone wrong. It's a disaster story in which the disaster is the failure to comprehend."

He added: "I've passed on to the reader some of the puzzlement and confusion of the characters in the book as they face a future with the alien."

That approach has led to a mixed reaction. The Guardian praised the book but said, external "it won't be for everyone", while the New York Times said, external: "The more we learn about the conditions of this novel's broken world, the harder it is to grasp."

The Literary Review described it as, external "a work of uncanny beauty, tender and terrifying in equal parts", while the Telegraph said, external "you feel you're not so much reading as dreaming".

Another Telegraph critic wrote, external that it was "ultimately, in both skill and humour, a cut above" the other shortlisted books.

"And in an age when AI overlords keep threatening to kill us, and the Government has told us to stockpile tinned food and bottled water, it is, for once, a novel that you can genuinely call 'timely'."

Speaking to BBC Radio 4's Today programme on Tuesday, Harrison explained how he had "wanted to write a book which really satirised the present-day barrage of information that we all suffer, without the necessary tools to understand what we're hearing and to analyse it and to have critical thinking about it".

He continued: "So the whole idea was to build a disaster in which it was a disaster of explanation, a disaster of the failure to understand the world as it was now."

articles.title: Tommy Walsh: Ground Force and Homes Under the Hammer star dies aged 69
articles.text:
Tommy Walsh, the building and DIY expert known for starring on TV shows including Ground Force, Homes Under the Hammer and Challenge Tommy Walsh, has died at the age of 69.

Walsh started his career as a professional builder before rising to fame alongside Alan Titchmarsh and Charlie Dimmock on the BBC's Ground Force from 1997 to 2005.

He went on to also front popular programmes including Clean It, Fix It, and Cowboys and Angels, and joined daytime TV favourite Homes Under the Hammer in 2021.

Walsh's agent told BBC News he died "peacefully after a long illness surrounded by his family", and asked for privacy for the family.

Walsh was previously reported to have had surgery for throat cancer in 2022 and lung cancer in 2023.

Walsh got his big break on TV after restoring the house of a BBC producer who was working on ideas for a show that would turn into Ground Force.

"She asked me to look at a couple of pilots. One of them was the precursor to Ground Force, called Over the Garden Wall," he told the BBC in 2004. "It was like watching paint dry - it was terrible."

Walsh said he initially turned down the chance to star on the show three times - but agreed when his eight-year-old daughter told him she had made a £10 bet with a boy at school that her dad was going to be on TV.

He found a winning formula with his co-stars, who performed makeovers on gardens belonging to members of the public.

His other shows included Tommy Walsh's Eco House, Tommy's DIY Survival, Trading Places, Space Invaders and Fix Your House For Free; and he published a number of DIY books.

articles.title: James Bond: What we know so far about the next 007 film
articles.text:
When a bartender asked James Bond in 2006's Casino Royale whether he'd like his vodka martini shaken or stirred, the irritated spy replied: "Do I look like I give a damn?"

Such throwaway lines were a clever way of signalling to the audience that this was a new era for 007 - and that the film series launched in 1962 was being overhauled with the arrival of Daniel Craig.

Over the next few films, producers struck a balance between nodding to the past while also moving away from some of the cheesier elements of the series, no longer sticking rigidly to all of the tradition and tropes of Bond.

"Were you expecting an exploding pen?" Ben Whishaw's Q later asked the secret service agent in Skyfall. "We don't really go in for that anymore."

Two decades on from Craig's debut, the series is about to be rebooted once again, with a new actor and new creative team. It's an exciting time for Bond fans as they wait to see what shape the next era will take. Here's what we know so far.

After years of speculation, the wheels are firmly in motion and we expect to hear who the new James Bond actor is in November or December.

Speaking in August, producer Amy Pascal told Deadline:, external "I would say the end of the year is a good bet. We are being really, really methodical."

The final screen tests reportedly took place in late October, so, unless something unexpected happens, it should not take much longer for producers to make their decision and the actor to sign the contract.

After that, it's just a matter of how the announcement will be made. In an earlier era, Bond actors were revealed with a traditional photo call or press conference.

But now that the franchise is owned by Amazon MGM, some expect the company to make the announcement via its own Prime Video streaming service.

The movie will be directed by Denis Villeneuve, known for Prisoners, Sicario, Arrival, Blade Runner 2049 and the recent Dune trilogy starring Timothée Chalamet.

"Some of my earliest movie-going memories are connected to 007," the French-Canadian director said last year. "I grew up watching James Bond films with my father, ever since Dr. No with Sean Connery. I'm a die-hard Bond fan. To me, he's sacred territory."

He added: "I intend to honour the tradition and open the path for many new missions to come. This is a massive responsibility, but also, incredibly exciting for me and a huge honour."

Bond 26 will be written by Steven Knight, known for TV series such as Peaky Blinders and House of Guinness, and films including Burnt, Spencer, Locke and The Girl in the Spider's Web.

Knight has said it had always been on his "bucket list" to write a Bond film, adding that he felt he was "doing my duty for King and country" by joining the franchise.

He told the BBC he planned to "write the character, not the actor", adding: "The thing with Bond is it's its own universe and franchise. So there are certain rules.

"Obviously you have to move it along, but I love where it sits. I love that it's British. I love that it's not DC or Marvel... So I feel a responsibility to the text."

Only six actors have played James Bond.

Sean Connery starred in six official Bond films between 1962 and 1971

George Lazenby starred in just one Bond film, in 1969

Roger Moore starred in seven Bond films between 1973 and 1985

Timothy Dalton starred in two Bond films, in 1987 and 1989

Pierce Brosnan starred in four Bond films, between 1995 and 2002

Daniel Craig starred in five Bond films between 2006 and 2021

You might have noticed some overlap in the above dates.

That's because Connery returned to the lead role for 1971's Diamonds Are Forever, after Lazenby took his place for 1969's On Her Majesty's Secret Service.

Connery also later appeared in 1983's Never Say Never Again, a Bond film produced by a different studio and not part of the official film series.

With the change in ownership and a new creative team now in place, the new Bond film is likely to make a fresh start.

It would be difficult to continue the story chronologically given the ending of 2021's No Time To Die, but that still leaves producers with plenty of options.

A different version of James Bond, who exists in a different universe, would be easily pulled off in an era where audiences are used to major film franchises restarting in a different world or timeline.

Bond 26 could even be set in a significantly earlier era - an idea that gained more popularity after Tony Gilroy revealed he and fellow director Steven Soderbergh previously pitched a 1960s version, external of Bond.

Separately, actor Ralph Fiennes recently said, external he had once been in talks to play Bond, and had suggested producers make a "black and white and very sort of film noir-y" version set in the 1950s.

Neither idea materialised, but the suggestion went down well with some Bond fans, who noted a period piece would help make the film truer to Ian Fleming's original character and books.

Exactly what shape the next film takes will become clear at a later stage. For now, fans are hoping that Christmas could be about to come early this year, as the world awaits the imminent announcement of the next actor to play 007.

articles.title: Shygirl: New album Swallow! is a chance to be more authentic
articles.text:
Hard-hitting beats, club anthems and unapologetically sexy lyrics are what Shygirl is known for.

But the singer and DJ - real name Blane Muise - has introduced a different sound for her second album, Swallow!, which dropped on Friday.

Shygirl hasn't totally left her electronic roots behind though.

You can still hear the sweat-soaked energy of Charli XCX's 365 remix and relentless pulse of 2024 hit mr useless on her latest record.

But there's also guitar strums, heartfelt songwriting and a dreamy haze, giving it an indie edge.

"I've learned over the 10 years I've been making music to have this confidence and to not be afraid of failure," she tells BBC Newsbeat.

"The big part of starting this record was wanting to have natural instrumentation and not feel like that was barred from me."

Shygirl puts the change down to a desire for a more "authentic" sound - a growing trend among British electronic artists who've been bringing a rockier influence to their music.

Asked why she took this musical direction, the 33-year-old says it was down to "the nostalgia of the indie sound".

"I felt the familiarity of that feeling, embracing the teenager within and the angst that I had and all the sounds that coloured that environment," she says.

Long-time producers Karma Kid and Casey MQ were "surprised" when Shygirl told them about her desire to work in more indie sounds, but she says the pair trusted her with the new direction.

Fans have been patiently waiting for something other than singles since her debut album Nymph was released in 2022.

The question now is whether they'll relate to this more rose-tinted version of Shygirl.

"It's not like I changed overnight," she insists. "In fact, it was because I was the girl I was in all the other songs that I became who I am now."

There are clear signs that Shygirl is entering a new chapter.

She cleared her Instagram feed before beginning the album rollout, and the artwork shows a bird hatching from an egg, symbolising rebirth.

But she points out the journey is an "evolution" rather than reinvention.

"I think it's less about moving away from me, but I would hate to repeat myself," she says.

"I would only wish to pick up the same tool if I felt like I had grown somewhat or had a renewed expertise for it."

That growth can be heard in tracks like Live the Life You Like - one of Shygirl's favourites on the album.

It features a gritty bassline and a manipulated riff that echoes a klaxon, which she describes as giving off "punk energy".

Leaning into that side of her sound has only made her more excited to take the record on a tour, starting with Europe in March.

"I've got a band now," she reveals with a grin. "I work with a drummer and a multi-instrumentalist and sometimes a bassist.

"It's just so fun to share the stage and be so inspired. We've rehearsed, but there's still so many moments for spontaneity and for us to look at each other and vibe."

Artists like PinkPantheress and Fred Again have also spoken about bringing indie influences into electronic music, something Shygirl says is "a reflection of what is going on in the world".

"I think there is a natural desire to have a sense of truth or something grounding," she says.

"And what is more grounding or more truthful than knowing exactly where a sound comes from."

So with artists borrowing more and more from across the musical spectrum, does genre still matter?

For Shygirl, it's less about what box listeners put her music in and more about whether it connects with them.

"Regardless if they like it or they hate it, I want someone to feel something. To be apathetic to my music would be the biggest insult to me."

articles.title: Jemima Goldsmith accuses Russell Brand of violence and abuse against her
articles.text:
Warning - this report contains graphic content.

Jemima Goldsmith, the ex-girlfriend of Russell Brand, has accused him of "violence, coercive control and abuse" while the two were together.

Goldsmith, who dated the disgraced entertainer for roughly a year around 2014, alleged that she "had to call the police to have him removed from my house in 2014 during a violent incident" but chose not to press charges.

In a lengthy statement on social media, the 52-year-old said she was "in awe of the courageous women who came forward at Brand's trial" and was "glad and relieved" he had "finally faced justice".

Brand, 51, was sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison earlier on Monday after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

He was found guilty of raping a woman at his home in 2009, as well as three counts of sexual assault against three other women.

The judge at the sentencing hearing told Brand that he harboured a "casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you", while his fame meant he believed "you could act when you liked and how you liked".

TV producer Goldsmith is also the former wife of ex-Pakistani prime minister and cricketer Imran Khan, the daughter of late billionaire entrepreneur Sir James Goldsmith and sister of ex-Conservative government minister Zac Goldsmith.

The mother-of-two said she had chosen not to pursue legal recourse against Brand over the alleged violent incident in 2014 as she was "worried about the impact of the press attention on my then teenage children".

She wrote on X on Monday evening: "Whilst my pain in relation to this pales in comparison to what the women have testified in court have suffered, this was a difficult period in my life which has had a lasting impact."

Goldsmith said she had not seen nor spoken to Brand since 2014, but claimed to have assisted the journalists who exposed the allegations against him and had been willing to testify to his "abusiveness" were they sued.

In her statement, she also addressed reports of an injunction taken out by her and Brand in October 2015 that banned a woman, Szilvia Berki, from harassing them including by making allegations of assault by Brand at Goldsmith's home the prior year.

Goldsmith said on Monday that Berki had visited her house for roughly 30 minutes on 7 June 2014 to give Brand a massage, which she said did not end up taking place once she arrived.

Goldsmith said that Berki later told police that Brand had pushed her in the back while she had been leaving and that she had been attacked by Goldsmith's dog. Brand's ex-girlfriend said she "did not see anything untoward" during the encounter.

She added that, after providing a statement and CCTV footage, police concluded that there was no case to answer.

Goldsmith accused Berki of then sending a series of "vicious antisemitic and threatening" messages and posting "wild and untrue allegations" about her on social media.

She said she then agreed to a suggestion from Brand's lawyer to seek an injunction to prevent harassment. She claimed on Monday that recent media reporting of the injunction had opened her up "to vile hatred and abuse online".

Sunday Times chief news correspondent Rosamund Urwin, who was involved in a media investigation into Brand in 2023, has told the BBC that Goldsmith helped her "a lot".

"I have seen the abuse she's been getting online and I did try to tell people that part of the story was much more complicated than they realise," Urwin said.

"I wish people would remember women that come forward are brave people and that is what she has done tonight – she has spoken out with immense bravery about how Russell Brand treated her," she added.

Brand's sentencing hearing heard victim impact statements from the women he had been accused of assaulting.

One of them said she was "upset and traumatised" for years after the incident, adding: "I didn't have any respect for myself. I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."

The woman he was found guilty of raping said the trauma was something she had to "carry every day".

A van believed to be carrying Brand was seen arriving at HMP Wandsworth in London on Monday after the sentencing hearing.

The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two-thirds point. In Brand's case, that would be seven years.

Once released, he is likely to spend the rest of his sentence on licence and will have to abide by specific rules such as wearing a tag.

The disgraced entertainer was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009 following a four-week trial at Southwark Crown Court.

He was found not guilty of two counts of rape and one count of attempted indecent assault.

articles.title: Russell Brand sentenced to 10-and-a-half years in prison for rape and sexual assault
articles.text:
Warning - this report contains graphic content.

Russell Brand has been sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison, after being convicted of rape and sexual assault.

In his sentencing remarks, judge Joel Bennathan described Brand as a "sexual predator" and criticised his "staggering arrogance".

The 51-year-old was sentenced to nine years for rape, with an additional 18 months, nine months and eight months for three counts of sexual assault.

The disgraced entertainer was found guilty of the charges involving four women between 2004 and 2009.

Brand did not react in the dock as he was sentenced. Before being taken down to the cells, he mouthed "I love you" to his wife Laura Brand, who was in the court.

The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two thirds point. In Brand's case that would be seven years.

Once released, he is likely to spend the rest of his sentence on licence and will have to abide by specific rules such as wearing a tag. His sentence will not be included in the early release scheme. Sex offenders, along with murderers, are exempt from the scheme.

The judge also paid tribute to the bravery of the women who gave evidence during the trial.

In further remarks, the judge said Brand's status protected him until 2023, when journalists from the Sunday Times, the Times and Channel 4's Dispatches outlined a series of misconduct allegations, leading to women making complaints to police.

He said Brand harboured a "casual arrogant disregard to any woman's right to say no to you", while his fame meant he believed "you could act when you liked and how you liked".

The judge said the evidence in the case also showed that Brand's entourage during the peak of his celebrity had "indulged your dreadful behaviour".

Before Brand's sentencing, the court heard victim impact statements from the women he had been accused of assaulting.

One of the women, who spoke from behind a screen, said she had been in "shock and turmoil for years".

"I was extremely upset and traumatised," she said. "I didn't have any respect for myself. I was thinking I was damaged goods - scared of giving off signals that could be taken the wrong way."

She added: "I just want to say - a leopard may change its spots but it's still a leopard."

"Russell Brand has managed to move on," a woman, who was sexually assaulted by Brand in 2005, said in a statement read out in court. "This has had a lasting impact on my life. I recognise this now.

"However, over the years, hearing his voice on television or seeing his image has made me jump. I had a strong adverse reaction hearing his voice."

She added: "Russell Brand is a sexual predator who has no remorse... I just hope he is not allowed to hurt any more women."

A statement from the woman Brand was found to have raped was also shared in court.

"I felt anxious, humiliated and overwhelmed," she said. "I struggled to sleep and eat, I struggled to cope with my emotions, I had to take time away from my work," she said.

She continued: "I had to live with my parents, I sought help and support... I am living with trauma, something I carry every day.

"My confidence and self esteem have been badly affected. I no longer trust my instincts."

The woman said one of the worst parts of what happened was her fear that she might have contracted HIV. She also said she was in considerable pain after the assault.

A woman, who was sexually assaulted while working on a Channel 4 project with Brand in 2009, said in a statement that she was "really upset" afterwards.

"I felt I lost my trust in people, I felt my working environment wasn't safe," she said. "I felt powerless in that moment and it had a knock-on effect on my confidence."

Brand's barrister Ian Winter KC put forward six character references, including one from Georgina Baillie, the granddaughter of the late actor Andrew Sachs.

Baillie was thrust into the spotlight in 2008 when Brand and Jonathan Ross left offensive messages about her on her grandfather's answering machine during a Radio 2 broadcast.

Winter also told the court that the former entertainer's wife Laura Brand, who gave evidence in her husband's defence during the trial, was experiencing "total devastation" at the verdicts.

He said Mr and Mrs Brand were "currently wrestling with how to exactly explain to a child who's just turned 10 what has happened here".

"It brings home the consequences of this conduct to totally innocent people who have been caught up in it," he said.

Sentencing Brand, the judge said: "I am very conscious that your imprisonment will deprive your children of the presence of their father.

"That sad loss to them, however, is caused by your serious offending."

articles.title: Ioan Gruffudd says 'explicit' images of him online are AI generated
articles.text:
Hollywood actor Ioan Gruffudd has warned fans of "explicit and disturbing" AI-generated content impersonating him online.

The 53-year-old star, from near Aberdare, Rhondda Cynon Taf, urged his followers not to send money to people using images and videos of his likeness, after the content was brought to his attention.

"A woman came to a convention I was recently attending and she was under the impression that she was in an extramarital relationship with me for over a year," he said in an Instagram post.

"She showed me hundreds of AI images and videos that someone claiming to be me had sent to her. The images were explicit and disturbing."

The actor said the woman had been targeted through a Facebook page dedicated to crime drama Elsbeth, in which Gruffudd played a musician named Angus.

Gruffudd, who rose to fame in the long-running Hornblower TV series, said a person behind the Facebook page had sent the woman "a cell number, and asked her to communicate via Telegram", an instant messaging app.

"'They began sending AI images and videos to 'prove' that it was me," Gruffudd added.

He said that if anyone believes they are speaking with him via social media pages that are not his official channels then "this is not me".

"I will never give out my cell number to anyone that I don't personally know.

"Please do not engage and never send money! I urge you to ignore and block all contact from anyone that claims to be me.

"Lastly, if you have been targeted by this person, please report them and their number to the police for investigation. I have done the same."

articles.title: Maya Jama steps down as host of reality TV show Love Island
articles.text:
Presenter Maya Jama has announced she is stepping down as the host of reality TV show Love Island after three years.

The 32-year-old wrote on Instagram alongside a highlights reel of her on the programme that it was "time to throw myself into something new".

"While my own Love Island journey has come to an end, I wish the show and the team all the success in the world, I'll be cheering you lot on from the sidelines forever," the TV and radio presenter said.

Jama's announcement comes hot on the heels of an appearance as a contestant on Celebrity Traitors that won her praise and speculation in the Times, external that she could "get £1m per deal" thanks to her success.

Thanking fans and the production team on Love Island, she said she had an "unforgettable time" on the programme.

"I started hosting the show aged 28 and during the nine incredible series met the most wonderful humans along the way. I've loved every slow-mo walk, fire pit and live show.

But she added: "I've always believed that to truly grow, you have to take a leap every now and then."

Jama landed her biggest presenting role to date as the host of the reality TV show in 2023, taking over from Laura Whitmore.

The programme couples contestants together who then complete a range of tasks and keep swapping in the hope of meeting the love of their life.

An ITV spokesperson said: "Maya has been a fantastic and much loved host on Love Island - we thank her for everything she has brought to the show over the last three years and wish her every continued success."

Love Island is one of the most popular reality TV shows in the UK but the series has polarised viewers, with some arguing the show is misogynistic and raising concerns about the welfare of contestants.

articles.title: Michael Ball's wedding surprise after BBC Radio 2 proposal
articles.text:
A couple whose surprise radio proposal captured hearts across the country were given an unforgettable wedding gift when singer and broadcaster Michael Ball turned up to perform at their ceremony.

Dawn Lloyd was shocked when her partner of more than 25 years Dave proposed on BBC Radio 2's Love Songs with Michael Ball programme in the summer and was stunned all over again when the presenter appeared at the couple's wedding at Weston Hall, in Stafford, on Sunday.

"I had no inkling whatsoever that this was going to happen," she said. "I was blown away.

"I just can't believe Dave has surprised me like this a second time. I was fooled the first time and now he has got me again."

Ball appeared without warning during the ceremony and performed Love Changes Everything, leaving Dawn and the wedding guests stunned.

Dawn said the day had been "perfect", with Dave adding he was "grateful for what Michael has done for us as a couple and for all of the family and friends to enjoy it as well".

articles.title: 'Time is up': Nandy warns media industry to take abuse seriously in wake of Brand case
articles.text:
Abuse in the media industry is probably still happening as organisations are not doing enough to protect women, the culture secretary has warned in the wake of Russell Brand's conviction.

Lisa Nandy told the BBC's Sunday with Laura Kuenssberg programme: "Time is up, it really is time for the media industry to take this seriously."

She added that since entering government, "many people" from within the industry had reached out to her "to allege that things have happened to them".

Brand is due to be sentenced on Monday after being convicted last week of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault, following allegations from multiple women spanning the decade between 1999 and 2009.

Nandy was asked whether she believed there was still exploitation and abuse within the media industry, following the Brand trial and cancellation of Channel 4 reality show Married at First Sight after the BBC revealed rape allegations.

She said: "I do not see that much has changed in terms of the way that institutions in the media industry and across public life, including politics, deal with women who very bravely come forward to allege abuse."

Nandy added that there was often no protection and a "very heavy cost" for women who speak up in industries such as media and politics, pointing to power imbalances and short-term contracts some staff members are given.

"Hand on heart, I can't say to you as the culture secretary that this is not happening today. In fact, if I had to wager, I would say it is," she said.

Nandy said many had come forward from within the industry, including from the BBC.

But she added that the BBC had been an "exemplar" in signing up to the industry body to protect whistleblowers - the Creative Industries Independent Standards Authority - and urged other organisations to follow suit.

A BBC spokesperson said the broadcaster "has made a significant commitment to improve its culture, processes and standards".

"Last year, following an independent culture review, we set out the behavioural expectations for everyone who works with or for the BBC and we were clear action would be taken if these were not met," the spokesperson added.
